en: *The Collected Subtleties of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle I (Compiled at Baiyun Monastery in the Guiwei year; this commentary may only be transmitted once it has been thoroughly examined and finalized).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Tanying of Qiantang:
Resolving the doubts of the multitude and giving rise to practice; benefiting all species with impartiality; nurturing both the holy and the ordinary;

encompassing both emptiness and existence—how could this ever transcend the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*? Asaṅga attained its verses through meditative concentration, and Vasubandhu received its commentary to complete it.
[The text] says: Were it not for the Compassionate Honored One of Tuṣita, who could have cleared the wilderness for the ultimate teaching?

Yet this scripture has a source of words so vast and profound, and an ocean of meaning so deep and unfathomable. Asaṅga (Asaṅga; here translated as "Non-attachment") repeatedly composed treatises to challenge and advance its study, and the Master of Wuxing further wrote commentaries to praise and expound upon it.
Having examined and discussed it in relation to the sūtra, the subtle mysteries have been fully exhausted; yet, while following the commentaries to verify the sūtra, [the task remains incomplete].
While the structural analysis (*kepan*) remains strictly adhered to, the explanations therein deviate from the underlying principles.

Thus, with no other recourse, I have ventured a "peep through a tube" at the meaning of Tiantai’s intent and traced the broad outlines of the treatise to compare them and clarify their respective merits and defects.

Furthermore, I have drawn upon Vasubandhu’s supplements as well as the strengths of both ancient and modern scholars; hence, it is titled *Caimei* (Gathering the Subtle), for it is a collection of gleanings.
(He-li qie). These various wonders are directly transcribed into this scripture, so that readers may find them easy to understand.
Written on the twenty-third day of the second month in the Renzi year of the Shaoxing era, while residing at the Lanya Hermitage in Sike.
Preface to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The commentary on the scripture is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the text. Regarding the explanation of the title, one surveys the general meaning of the entire scripture to interpret its opening heading.

This "general meaning" consists of fivefold profound principles (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*), namely: name (*nāma*), essence (*svabhāva*), purport (*śāstra*), function (*kriyā*), and the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*).
First, regarding the explanation of the name, the metaphor and the dharma constitute the name. *Vajra* (Diamond) is the metaphor; *Prajñā* (Wisdom), etc., are the dharma. *Vajra*...

Regarding "the firm" (*kaṭhina*), the commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* presents two interpretations: first, in relation to the diamond jewel (*vajra-ratna*); second, in relation to the painted form of the vajra.
To begin with, regarding the diamond jewel: this jewel originates from the country of India. In the Sanskrit language it is called *vajra*, also known as *khaḍgara*.
This is translated here as "diamond," meaning that which is the most refined and solid among gold. The "firm" (*kaṭhina*) arises within gold.

Tempered a hundred times, it cannot be melted; it can cut jade. Because it is taken for its hardness and sharpness to be able to sever and destroy all things—just as *prajñā* can sever all delusions—it is used as a metaphor.
My Patriarch said: "Prajñā is like a diamond (*vajra*); wherever it is applied, everything is shattered. Asaṅga said:
"That which is able to sever [delusions] is that which is heard, contemplated, and cultivated within the *prajñāpāramitā*."

It is severed. It is severed at the point where a vajra severs. If that is so, since all Prajñāpāramitā sūtras such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* possess the power to sever, why is this sūtra alone compared to a vajra? Answer:

It is precisely because prior to this assembly, during the sessions of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, the Buddha had caused all sentient beings to abide in this Prajñā. Therefore, [the Buddha]...
The lineage of the Buddha-nature is unbroken, yet there is the entrustment through protective mindfulness. However, those who hear this will surely harbor doubts:
"The Prajñā is the fruit; it is the Dharma in which the Buddhas abide. Sentient beings have heavy defilements—how can they possibly abide therein? This serves to subdue their distraction.

Although the assembly has been subdued in their doubts, they have not yet attained resolution. When Subhūti arrived here, for the sake of severing the doubts of the multitude, he recounted his former sighs of lamentation.

Questioning the matter of abiding through subduing, the Buddha answered in order to dispel doubts; thus, he causes those who abide in this *prajñā* to be like a diamond (*vajra*) capable of severing afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, the Treatise states (hereafter, the treatise refers to the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-āloka* by Asaṅga): "This minor diamond *pāramitā*..."
The power is manifested by such names; the power of *prajñā* is manifested by such names of the *vajra*.
Therefore, one should know that whatever constitutes *prajñā*, it all possesses this power. Since this is a commentary on the various *prajñās* that resolves doubts, [it is so stated].
Therefore, although the two characters "Vajra" appear here in the text, their meaning actually serves as a universal metaphor for all Prajñāpāramitās.
Consequently, those who uphold and recite them gain profound merit and deep efficacy. Second, regarding the drawing of its form, as the treatise says:
"Furthermore, it is like drawing the form of a vajra, which is wide at the beginning and end, but narrow in the middle; such is the Prajñāpāramitā, which is [narrow] in the middle..."

The "narrow" refers to the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*). The "broad at the beginning and end" refers to the Stage of Faithful Practice (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) and the Tathāgata Stage (*tathāgatabhūmi*).
This demonstrates the meaning of non-commonality (*āveṇika-artha*). The commentary states: Thus, the vajra-pestle of a strongman possesses the power to destroy objects.
This may be compared to the stages (bhūmi) of this sutra. Thus, the sixteen abodes are collectively termed the Stage of Practice through Faith (śraddhācaryā-bhūmi).
The eighteenth, the higher seeking of the Buddha-ground, is termed the Tathāgata-ground. Within the higher seeking of the Buddha-ground, there are further six kinds of fulfillments;
within the fulfillment of the sixth mind, there are again six meanings. In this way, the beginning and the end are wide apart, while the middle [is narrow].
In this interval, there is only the seventeenth stage, the dwelling place of entering the path of realization, named the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*). This is what is meant by "narrow.
Therefore, it is like the form of a vajra. As for the specific mention of "painting," it is said because this jewel does not exist here, but only painted images are transmitted.
Since this meaning corresponds to the stages (*bhūmi*), it is found specifically in this sutra and its treatises; that is to say, it is made manifest.
To demonstrate the meaning of "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) is to clarify the initial intention: that it is shared with all *prajñās*.
Regarding *prajñā*, there are some who provide a translation, calling it "wisdom" (*hui-zhi*); others leave it untranslated, because it gives rise to the wholesome. Mount Gu Shan states:
"The reason 'wisdom' is not used is that *prajñā* is a term of the heavens (*deva*), while 'wisdom' is a term of humans. Heavenly terms are revered; human terms are trivial."
The intention is to preserve the original virtue of the term. It has not been translated since ancient times; now, when we speak of *prajñā*, it must necessarily comprise three types:

namely, *upāya-prajñā* (skillful means wisdom), *vipaśyanā-prajñā* (contemplative insight wisdom), and *dharmatā-prajñā* (wisdom of the true nature of reality). Thus, the general title serves as a heading for the specific texts.

Consequently, one can understand by implication that all three types are present beneath every section of the text. The commentary states: "According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two types."
Prajñā refers to mundane prajñā and supramundane prajñā. The mundane consists of seeking the fulfillment of knowledge solely within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The supramundane consists of being free from mental attachment even toward [virtues such as] generosity and ethical discipline.
Because even the concentrated mind and the distracted mind are ultimately unattainable, one should know that those who rely on the Tripiṭaka primarily cultivate mundane *prajñā*.
This is illustrated by the case of the minister Gopāla, who divided the land to settle disputes; such is the nature of their practice.

In the Mahāyāna gate, one correctly cultivates supramundane *prajñā*, for through contemplation one realizes that the causes and conditions of giving and so forth are empty, and that neither their essential nature nor their characteristics can be apprehended.
Therefore, within the Mahāyāna gate, there are both common and uncommon Prajñās. Furthermore, this applies across the various divisions of the teachings.

If categorized by division, the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) Prajñā is called "common," because it is shared with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The *Avataṃsaka* is called "uncommon," because this scripture does not fall into the hands of those of the two vehicles.
If categorized by teaching, it specifically belongs to the fourth period; for the *Prajñā* division is pervasive [throughout].

Regarding the three teachings: in the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the three vehicles study together; thus it is called the "Shared Teaching" (*gongjiao*). In the Distinct and Perfect Teachings, the two vehicles do not hear [these doctrines];

thus they are called the "Unshared Teachings" (*bujingjiao*). Jingxi said: "Therefore, these two 'sharings' both share with the two vehicles; this refers to the two types of sharing: that of the *bun* (division/section) and that of the teaching.

This sutra properly concerns the teaching according to its classification (*yuejiao*), rather than the meaning of the division. Question: According to the classification by teaching, does it belong to the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*)? It possesses [all four].
There are four teachings, which should likewise receive the names "common" and "uncommon. Why, then, are they specifically situated in the fourth period? Answer:
Jingxi says that because the Vaipulya (fangdeng) sutras mostly follow the method of refutation and censure (*tanhe*), their common meaning is somewhat sparse. Question:

Regarding the two types of Prajñā—the common and the uncommon—were they heard by the same assembly in a single session, or were they preached at different seats? If it was a single session, then [the distinctions between] the Separate and the Perfect would also...

Regarding the two vehicles: if they occupy different seats, the *Prajñā* [teachings] universally encompass the three vehicles. Answer: Since the various sections of the *Prajñā* universally encompass the three vehicles, the two vehicles sit together;
yet although they hear the Separate and Perfect [teachings], they do not understand them, as they lack the cause for receiving their nourishment.
This state is like being deaf and mute. Therefore, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) states:

"The various versions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* teach the uncommon dharmas of the two kinds of Middle Way—the 'only' and the 'not-only'—together with the Two Vehicles. If this were so, it would merely be a common teaching; it would not be a common realization."
Pāramitā. This is translated as "reaching the other shore" (*pāra-gata*). It is also called "the infinite crossing" (*du wu ji*) or "the ultimate fulfillment of the task.

*Sūtra* is a general name. In Sanskrit, it is *sūtra*, which is translated in meaning as "scripture" (*jing*). It is called a "scripture" because it has passed through the minds and mouths of the sages.
It is also called a "scripture" even when there is no direct equivalent, for the six classics spoken by the sages of this land are so designated.

The term "sūtra" (經) is used here to represent that which was spoken by the Dharma King; it is likewise called a sūtra. In the Tiantai school’s interpretation of sūtras, there are generally three aspects considered:
teaching, practice, and principle. As the sūtra says: "Those who copy, read, and recite [it]" refers to the sūtra of teaching (教經).
"Those who believe, understand, accept, and uphold [it]" refers to the sūtra of practice (行經). "All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emerge from this sūtra" refers to the sūtra of principle (理經).
Although it is categorized into three types, the title of the work refers specifically to the *sūtra* as the teaching that expresses [the meaning] (*śāsana*).
Practice and principle are what are expressed by that teaching. Tiantai said: "In foreign lands, *sūtra* is the general name for the holy teachings. Jingxi said:
"The entire body of teachings throughout one Buddha’s lifetime is all called *sūtra*. This concludes the explanation of the name. As for the other four chapters, they are the actual...

The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) constitute its essence (*śarīra*), because they are what is expounded throughout the entire sūtra. The perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) constitutes its primary tenet (*mukhya-artha*), because the meaning of giving subsumes all six perfections and represents the essential practice cultivated throughout the sūtra.
Its function (*karman*) is to destroy the two types of grasping—clinging to persons and phenomena—because every passage of the text washes away all conceptual marks (*nimitta*).

The Mahāyāna constitutes its doctrinal characteristic (*upadeśa-lakṣaṇa*), because it possesses the flavor of refined butter (*ghṛta*). If one proceeds according to the title, then it subsumes the three Prajñās as a whole.

As for the name: "Contemplative Observation" (Guānzhào) corresponds to its essential principle (zōng). "True Reality" (shíxiàng) and "Skillful Means" (fāngbiàn) allow one to understand its essence (tǐ) and function (yòng). This is what is meant by "explaining the name":

it takes these three dharmas—essence, principle, and function—and correlates them respectively with the three aspects of totality and particularity (sānyī zǒngbié). Is this not precisely what is being described?
△ Second, the explanation of the text. Now, following Asaṅga’s classification of the sūtra into eighteen stages (*vihāra*), the remaining detailed items are all derived from the commentary.
Furthermore, where necessary, supplementary notes from the sub-commentaries have been added, with appropriate discretion; there is sound reasoning underlying these choices.
Question: When the Bodhisattva Asaṅga entered the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* (Sunlight Samādhi) and ascended to Tuṣita, he personally [encountered] Maitreya...

He received the *Eighty Verses* (*Aṣṭadaśaka*) from his honored teacher. For what purpose did he further compose a treatise? He composed the *Explanation of the Eighteen Abodes* (*Aṣṭādaśasthānavyākhyāna*) to comment upon the sūtra.

Answer: The *Eighty Verses* merely recite the text of the sūtra directly; it lacks a formal structural analysis (*vibhāga*). Consequently, the sequence of the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) and its underlying intent remain unclear.
For this reason, he separately composed a treatise to provide a comprehensive exposition. Question: The *Eighty Verses* are divided into twenty-seven sections (*pariccheda*).
A doubt arises: "The veins and arteries flow smoothly; why is there no sequential order? Answer: "The division of the text and its structural analysis were intended by Vasubandhu;
Asaṅga obtained only his verses. Question: "Can these two treatises be reconciled? Answer: "There is no need.

Since the meaning of the sutra is manifold, each takes up a particular sense for its own commentary. This sutra is divided into three sections; the first section of the text extends from 'Thus have I heard' up to 'the seats were spread.'"
and sat down. This is the introductory section (*nidāna*). From the passage "The Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat in the great assembly" onwards is the main body (*śarīra*) of the teaching.
If, as the commentators maintain, this text were assigned to a separate introduction (*pratyuddeśa*), then that separate introduction would merely serve to manifest the main body;
if it did not manifest what is to be expressed, the meaning of an "introduction" would not be established. Now, assigning this text to the main body means that [the assembly] rose from their seats...

It arises; although not yet explicitly stated, the matter must pertain to the correct [teaching]. Rising from one’s seat is due to the request for the Dharma. Third, the passage beginning with "Subhūti, if there be anyone...

and so forth belongs to the Section on Dissemination (*Prasāraṇa-bhāga*). The Commentary states that this refers to conduct and dwelling without defilement, which is precisely the unblemished propagation [of the teaching].
Furthermore, the introduction (*nidāna*) has both general and specific distinctions. The general introduction is common to the Way of the Three Times, as evidenced by the present...

Because all the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras of the Buddha’s single lifetime contain such phrases as these, the separate prefaces (nidāna) differ according to the specific gate of teaching and the particular faculties of the audience, while the sūtras themselves differ in their respective vehicles and conditions. As for the general preface (sādhāraṇa-nidāna), when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda requested four matters;
the Buddha then commanded that the words "Thus have I heard" and so forth be placed at the beginning of all sūtras.
Upon seeing these words, one believes them to be the Buddha’s teaching; therefore, they are called the "Preface of Verified Faith" (*saddharmapratyayāvatāra*).

Alternatively, they are called the "Preface Prior to the Sūtra," because the Tathāgata, before entrusting all sūtras, commanded that these words be placed at their beginning. Or they are called the "Preface Subsequent to the Sūtra," because they were only added at the time of the communal recitation (*saṃgīti*).
Or they are called the "Preface for Refuting the Erroneous," because it serves to refute the heterodox views of outsiders such as Āyu. This [refers to] the preface of this sūtra.
There are six matters; thus, one is separated from the Buddha and his dwelling place. This is divided into six parts. △ First, the principle transmitted:
it is as follows.
Master Zhao stated: "Thus" (*evam*) is a term of faith and compliance. Through faith, the principles one has heard are harmonized;
through compliance, the way between teacher and disciple is perfected. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The meaning of 'thus' is precisely faith.
If there is pure faith within a person's mind, that person can enter the Buddha-dharma; if there is no faith, that person cannot enter the Buddha-dharma."
Regarding the Dharma: those who lack faith say that such matters are not so; those who have faith say that such matters are indeed so.

One without faith is like an ox-hide that has not been softened, which cannot be bent or folded. One with faith is like an ox-hide that has already been softened, which can be fashioned according to its use.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras that faith is a hand; just as a person with hands may enter a treasury of jewels...
In a mountain, one may take jewels at will; so it is with those who possess faith. They enter the mountain of the Dharma-jewels and take whatever they desire at their own disposal.

Those without faith are like people without hands: even if they enter a mountain of jewels, they cannot take any, and because they lack hands, they are instead harmed by the jewels as they move about. So it is with those without faith who enter the Buddha-Dharma.
The Jewel Mountain: it is not merely that nothing is obtained; because of a lack of faith, one slanders the Dharma and falls into suffering.
It is precisely because of such faith that there is what is heard. My Patriarch said: "That which is thus is the very essence of the Dharma as heard throughout this entire section.
II. The Person Capable of Transmitting [the Teaching].
I have heard that Master Zao said: "Those who clarify the production of the scriptures personally received the holy intent; thus, there is no error of hearsay.

However, at the time of the compilation, Ānanda had already eliminated craving and attachment, and both forms of selfhood were exhausted. That he now uses the word 'I' is for the purpose of transmitting the Dharma."

Therefore, in accordance with worldly convention, we use the provisional designation "I. Regarding "hearing," the *Mahā-śāstra* states that when the faculty of the ear is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and there is an act of attention directed toward hearing, then the faculty, the object, and the mind converge; thus, hearing occurs.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In accordance with worldly convention, we speak of a 'self,' and the designation 'hearing' arises from a combination [of factors].

However, when Ānanda ascended the high seat to compile the teachings, Mahākāśyapa held up his *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) and paid him reverent homage with such earnestness that he was no different from the Buddha.
When the great assembly witnessed this, they each harbored doubts, thinking: 'Since Kāśyapa serves as the refuge for the fourfold assembly, he is not the Buddha.'"
It is not so. Now, regarding this act of prostration: one might wonder, "Has he ceased his reverence and departed? Or one might doubt, "Has a Buddha from another direction arrived?
Or one might doubt, "Is Ānanda seated upon the high throne; has Ānanda attained Buddhahood? Thus, it should be known that these three doubts arise simultaneously, produced by Kāśyapa’s prostration.
By uttering once, "Thus have I heard," it is known that this is the formal collection (saṃgīti) out of reverence for the Dharma.
According to the ritual, the three doubts are immediately stilled. Traditionally, it has been said that these were "provisional doubts," intended to inspire future faith and sincerity.
If this were so, one should have doubted only Ānanda’s attainment of Buddhahood; why was there need for these two [additional] doubts? Alternatively, they may be called "actual doubts."
Because Ānanda ascended the seat, his appearance resembled that of the Buddha; since the assembly did not recognize him, they were doubtful.

If this were so, they should have merely doubted that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni had emerged again or that a Buddha from another direction had arrived—why would they need to doubt that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood?

Nevertheless, how should one understand the provisional and the real in this context? It must be understood that since [the event] occurred through Kāśyapa’s prostration, the matter defied ordinary expectations, and the assembly...
Consequently, doubt arose; this was indeed a genuine doubt. △ Third, regarding the time when the principle was realized:
it should properly state "on such a month and day. This is because the three seasons of that land and the four seasons of this region differ in their annual cycles.

It cannot be translated [literally]. However, to describe the beginning and end of the preaching of the sutra, it is generally termed "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), which refers to the moment when the fourfold assembly was moved by the teaching and attained benefit. △ Fourth, the Master who Received the Teaching.
Regarding "Buddha," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Buddha" means "the Knower. What phenomena does he know?

It refers to all dharmas—namely, the categories of sentient beings and non-sentient things throughout the three periods of time, as well as the permanent and the impermanent—and so forth. He fully and clearly awakened to these beneath the Bodhi tree.

Because he knows [all things], he is named Buddha. However, beneath a single tree, there is one Buddha; yet according to the capacities of those taught by the four teachings, there appear four Buddhas with differing physical characteristics.
Since this is a Mahāyāna sūtra, we shall now discuss three Buddhas. △ Fifth, the place where it was heard.
"In Śrāvastī. "In" means dwelling. "Śrāvastī" is correctly called *Śrāvastī*; it is a corruption of that term, also rendered as *Śāvatthī*.

In a new translation, it is rendered as "Abundant Virtue," meaning that the country abounds in four things: first, material wealth; second, sensory objects; third, [the Dharma]; and fourth, [the Sangha].

"Much-heard" (*bahuśruta*). Regarding "objects of hearing" (*wenwu*), the old translations rendered it as such. The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* states: "There is nothing that is not there; the whole world hears of it;
therefore it is called 'objects of hearing. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Because the Buddha knows gratitude, he dwells frequently in Rājagṛha and Śrāvastī.
He dwells in Śrāvastī to repay the debt of gratitude for the land where his birth-body was born, and [he dwells in Rājagṛha] to repay the debt of gratitude for the Dharma."
Because of the kindness of his physical body, he resided in Rājagṛha; for the Dharma-body is superior to the birth-body, he dwelt more frequently in Rājagṛha than in the other city.
Question: The Sūtra states that he was born in the country of Kapilavastu; why then does the Śāstra say he was born in Śrāvastī? Answer:
The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that Kapila and Śrāvastī were adjacent to one another, both being within Central India.
This is stated because of the [specific] circumstances. Question: The country of Kapilavastu is the birthplace of the Buddha; for what reason did he not dwell there for long?

Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: When the Buddha first returned to his country, the thousand bhikṣus who were the brothers of Kāśyapa had originally practiced the Brahmanical methods and performed austerities in the mountains; their appearance was haggard and emaciated. When the father-king saw these bhikṣus...

"Kauṭilya, you are not worthy to adorn and honor the World-Honored One. Instead, select the sons and younger brothers of the noble Śākyas, as well as those of robust households, and dispatch one person from each by force to enter the monastic life. Among them, some will have virtuous hearts and delight in the Path, while others will not.
These Śākya bhikṣus should not remain in their native places. Why is this? Since they have not yet abandoned desire, if they remain near their kinsmen,"
Because thoughts of defiled attachment would inevitably arise, he did not dwell much in the kingdom of Kapilavastu for the sake of protecting such people.
As for Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma:
"Jetavana" is the Sanskrit *Jetavana*, also called *Jeta*; its correct pronunciation is *Śreṣṭha*, which translates here as "Victorious in Battle."
He was also the crown prince of King Prasenajit. In the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra*, he is referred to as "the tree of the Śākya clan. Regarding Anāthapiṇḍada:
in Sanskrit he is called Sudatta, which translates here as "Giver to the Destitute" (Anāthapiṇḍada); he is also named "Good Giver" (Śubhadatta).

Because this elder was compassionate and constantly provided for the destitute and orphaned, and because he was skilled at practicing generosity, the people of the country addressed him by this title. (From the *Nanshan [Luoyang Qianfusi Shizun Shengjiao Xu]*).
According to the *Linggan zhuan* (Account of Inspired Visions): "The site of Jetavana Monastery measured only ten *li* from east to west and seven *li* plus seventy paces from north to south.
Initially, Sudatta went to the Prince to purchase the garden. The Prince said: 'If you can cover the ground with gold, [the land shall be yours].'"
"Let there be no interval of delay; we shall then proceed together. Sudatta replied, "I agree," and followed the price set.
The Prince said, "This was merely a jest. Sudatta said, "One should not speak falsely. They immediately entered into a legal dispute.

At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed himself into a man and adjudicated, saying, "According to the law of the Prince, one should not speak falsely. Since the price has already been settled, it is improper to retract now."
[Ananda] regretted it. The Prince then gave it to him. He immediately had people load the gold onto elephants and carry it out of the park.
In a short while, it was nearly full, with only a small area remaining. Sudatta thought to himself, "Which storehouse would have enough gold that is neither too much nor too little to fill this spot?
He asked Jeta, "Do you regret selling it at such a high price? [Jeta] replied, "No. I am simply considering which storehouse would suffice; I shall fill it."
He filled it to the brim. Jeta thought to himself, "The Buddha must be of great virtue, for he can cause this man to regard his treasure as so light.
Thinking thus, he said, "Stop here; do not offer any more gold. Let the grounds of the garden belong to you, but let the trees belong to me. I shall offer them myself to the Buddha."
He proceeded to erect a vihāra and build a dwelling for the Buddha, using exquisite sandalwood as fragrant plaster.
He prepared one thousand two hundred separate rooms for residence, and at each of these one hundred and twenty locations, he installed a *gaṇḍī* (a wooden board struck like a bell in this region).
Having completed these arrangements, he invited the Buddha to reside there. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Now, regarding this park..."
They established it at the location he had designated. With the trees, flowers, and fruits belonging to Jetavana, the two men, being of one mind, together founded a vihāra.
It should be called "Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. To honor the ruler first and the subject later is the way of propriety. △ Sixth, the companions who heard and upheld [the Dharma].
He was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

"Together with" (yǔ) means "in company with. "Great" (dà) is an exclamation of praise for his virtues. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "mahā" is translated as "great," "many," or "superior."
It is "Great" (*Mahā*) because it is revered by great beings such as the celestial kings; "Many" (*Bahu*) because it encompasses the four Vedas and the three Piṭakas;
and "Victorious" (*Vibhu*) because it surpasses the ninety-five types of non-Buddhist paths. The translator followed one [of these meanings] and simply called it "Great."

"Monk" (*bhikṣu*) may alternatively be translated as "one who eliminates hunger. Sentient beings, while in the causal stage, lack the means to sustain themselves and thus receive retributions that are largely characterized by scarcity and want.
The monastic life of precepts and conduct is a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); it can produce wholesome qualities and eliminate the hunger of cause and effect.

Alternatively, there is no direct equivalent for the term. Herein lie three meanings: "mendicant" (*yācanaka*), "one who destroys evil" (*pāpavināśaka*), and "one who terrifies Māra" (*māratarjana*). He neither looks upward nor looks downward.
Neither square nor bound, he is free from these four kinds of nutriment. Proceeding on alms-round in due order, he sustains his life with purity; therefore, he is called a "beggar" (*bhikṣu*).
By observing the seven branches of the precepts, he chains the monkey-mind with meditation, fears the wolf of impermanence, and removes the fat of afflictions;
this is called "destroying evil. Because he cultivates this Dharma, the celestial Māras feel vexed and poisoned; they fear he will transcend their realm and dread that he will deliver others.

Therefore, there is sorrow and fear. Although there are three meanings [to this], the eradication of evil is fundamental. Regarding the term "assembly" (*saṃgha*): according to various sūtras, the word "assembly" appears in all instances;
four or more persons in harmonious union constitute an assembly. As for the phrase "together with twelve hundred and fifty persons":
the three Kāśyapa brothers together numbered one thousand, while Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana together numbered two hundred and fifty.

The master and his disciples returned to the Buddha and both became his followers. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "For what reason do these bhikṣus always follow the World-Honored One? It answers:
"They are like a patient who, having recovered, constantly follows a great physician; they are like the myriad stars bowing toward the moon, manifesting the Buddha’s venerable virtue.
Because they heard the various sūtras together, this [group] is singled out for mention. △ Second, the specific introduction.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in his robes and taken up his alms bowl at the hour of eating, entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
This prologue initiates the sutra. As for "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān), he is endowed with the ten titles and is honored by the world.
"At the hour of eating" refers to the forenoon. In the *Vīrasamādhi-sūtra*, the Buddha expounds the four kinds of nutriment for the Bodhisattva Dharmamati.
At that time, the devas eat at dawn; the Buddhas of the three periods of time eat at midday; the animals eat in the late afternoon; and the ghosts and spirits eat at dusk.
As for "putting on robes," he puts on the *saṃghāṭī*. As for "carrying an almsbowl," he carries the bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings.
As for "entering the city," the monastery was located five or six *li* outside the city; since he wished to beg for food, he had to enter the city.
This is because the Buddha personally went on almsround for six reasons: first, so that the blind might obtain sight;
second, so that women obstructed by their parents might obtain sight; third, so that the sick might obtain sight; fourth, to establish a model;
fifth, to eliminate pride, ensuring that no one feels contemptuous toward those they see; and sixth, to demonstrate the bowl of the Heavenly King.
Therefore, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "One should divide the food into four portions: first, set aside a portion to give to fellow practitioners of the holy life;
second, set aside a portion to bestow upon the poor, the sick, and beggars; third, give it to sentient beings of water and land; fourth, eat it oneself."

Having gone on his alms-round through the city in due order, he returned to his original place. When he had finished his meal, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.
Regarding "alms-round by successive order," the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "All Buddhas of the past all practiced alms-round by successive order without making any selection.
Regarding "collecting the robe and bowl": when washing the feet, it is necessary to collect the robes. As for "washing the feet," it is as the saying goes:
washing the hands is called *guàn*, washing the head is called *mù*, washing the body is called *yù*, and washing the feet is called *xǐ* (pronounced xiàn). Why is this so?
First one eats, and afterwards washes the feet. One should know that upon returning from begging for alms, there is a fear that the time [for the meal] will have passed;

therefore, one eats first. Only after finishing the meal does one wash the feet. As the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "At noon, if the shadow of the sun passes by even the width of a hair or a single moment, it is no longer the proper time.
Regarding "spreading out a seat and sitting," the *Śāstra* asks: For what reason did the World-Honored One [adopt] the deportment of one who is in a state of tranquility?
"Sitting" indicates that he who manifests only tranquility is able to awaken to and expound the Dharma;

because he is endowed with merit and wisdom, he is able to awaken to and expound it, and thus his teaching does not arise in vain. "Displaying the cross-legged posture" indicates that he awaits those who will inquire.
Now, why is alms-seeking made the primary theme of this sutra? One must understand that sequential begging for alms symbolizes non-abiding in marks (*animitta*). As for eating...

The act of sitting after finishing [the meal] symbolizes abiding in the principle of quiescence. Furthermore, begging for food constitutes the *zhāi* (fast); *zhāi* signifies "to align. By aligning the mind with objective phenomena, one manifests the true teaching.
Within the six perfections and myriad practices, the mind and its objects are brought into equilibrium. Regarding this, there are those who correlate these acts with the three trainings (*triśikṣā*).
What sūtra does this not elucidate? This is far too broad and diffuse.
△ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching. According to the treatise, there are seven thematic phrases (*arthapada*). Now, based on the first three phrases, the text is divided into three sections.
First, the non-interruption of the single lineage; second, the mode of initiating practice; third, the locus where practice resides. Regarding the first, there are two parts.
First, the aspect of reverence:
At that time, the Elder Subhūti was among the great assembly.

Elder, in the Āgamas, the Buddha said: "O bhikṣus, from now on, those who are senior shall be addressed as 'Mahāsthavira' (Great Virtuous One), and those who are junior shall be addressed as 'Sthavira' (Elder).
The title 'Sthavira' does not necessarily imply advanced age. Thus, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra cites a verse:
"What is called the mark of an elder Is not necessarily due to being old in years. One may have a thin frame with white hair, Yet be empty of virtue within; such a one is merely aged."

(Refuting the incorrect view: One who is able to relinquish the fruits of both sin and merit, who practices the holy life with diligence, and who has already detached from all phenomena—such a person is called an "Elder" (*sthavira*).
(Revealing the correct view: This is merely a way of praising one's virtuous deeds; even if one is advanced in years, if they lack inner virtue, they are still termed "young.
As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: although Ānanda’s hair had turned white, Kāśyapa referred to him as "young. Now...

As for those who are so called: Subhūti is both virtuous and long-lived; he possesses these two excellences. Subhūti is translated as "Born of Emptiness" (Kongsheng), and is also called "Excellent Appearance" (Shanxian) or "Auspiciousness" (Shanjí).
This name was established because at the time of his birth, the granaries, treasuries, chests, and vessels in his household were all empty.
Diviners declared that the signs manifested were both excellent and auspicious, and thus the name was given. However, his granaries and treasuries were entirely empty.
What is meant by "auspicious" (*kṣaya*)? One should know that at the moment of arising, it is momentarily empty, yet immediately returns to its original state.

Thus, although it is empty, it is sufficient for immediate use; this indicates the subsequent understanding of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), wherein although it is empty, all phenomena are fully present.
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder.

There are two types of baring the shoulder: if it occurs in this region, it is for the purpose of apologizing for one’s offenses, as in the *Zuozhuan* account where the Marquis of Zheng, when surrounded by the King of Chu and subsequently defeated, bared his flesh and led a sheep. If it occurs in that region, it is for the purpose of...
Regarding ritual etiquette: when a disciple attends upon a teacher, whether arriving at the teacher’s location or otherwise, he must bare the right shoulder and cover the left.
This is done out of concern that the teacher may have instructions to give, so as to facilitate ease of movement during manual labor.
Place the right knee on the ground.
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "The right is the correct path; the left is the deviant path. Employ the correct to eliminate the deviant. The *Baihutong* says:
"Heaven rotates to the left, while the sun, moon, and five planets move to the right. Therefore, to accord with worldly custom, one uses the right knee."

He touches the ground with his knees. If one discusses what is symbolized: the knees symbolize practice (*caryā*), and the earth symbolizes principle (*tattva*). Because practice accords with principle, the knees touch the ground.
He joins his palms in reverent homage.
Joining the palms together like the hands folded in the secular world signifies respect. Master Zhaoluo said: "This is the manner of requesting the Dharma.
△ Second, addressing the Buddha, which has two parts. First, expressing admiration.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One!

It should be known that prior to this assembly, I had already heard various Prajñāpāramitās; thus, my doubts remained suppressed within my breast, for there was no means by which they might be resolved.
Now, beholding this manifestation of sitting in tranquility, I know for certain that you intend to bestow the Dharma upon us for eternity, in order to clarify what is appropriate."

Because one attains this Prajñā, the meaning of the lineage of the Buddhas being uninterrupted. Elder Subhūti, at the beginning of the sutra, offered an exclamation of rare wonder to the World-Honored One.
II. Narrating the Events: This narrates the matters previously seen and heard.
The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas.

Regarding "skillfully protecting and sustaining": for those bodhisattvas who are already mature, the Buddha provides protection and sustenance through his power of skillful means, guarding their mindfulness so that they do not lose their wholesome benefits.
Regarding "skillfully entrusting": for those bodhisattvas who are not yet mature, the Buddha then commits them to others.
Entrustment: Those bodhisattvas who have already reached maturity shall, in future ages, bring others to maturity through *prajñā*.
For this reason, the Tathāgata protects and entrusts them so that the lineage of the Buddhas (*buddhagotra*) shall never be interrupted.
Regarding "bodhisattva," it is the Sanskrit term *mahā-bodhi-sattva*; here, for brevity, the remainder is omitted and it is simply called "bodhisattva."
This is translated as "the mind that accomplishes sentient beings through the Great Way. It is also called "Opening Being" (Kāśyapa) and "Great Courageous Mind," among others.
△ Second, the characteristics of the arousal of practice: Subhūti rose from his seat; having first paid homage and offered praise, he subsequently posed his question.
This is the ritual protocol. Herein there are three parts. First, Subhūti initiates the inquiry:
"World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide?
How should they subdue their minds?"
*Anuttara*: this is translated as "unsurpassed. *Samyak-saṃ*: this is translated as "right and equal. *Bodhi*: this is translated as "awakening.
Thus, it is the mind of unsurpassed right and equal awakening. Only one who has generated this mind proceeds in the practice of *prajñā*.

Although doubts were previously suppressed, they are now permitted to be raised as questions. It is from this that the characteristics of the sūtra arise. The treatise asks: For what reason does Subhūti...

Questioning also has six causes and conditions: first, for the sake of severing doubt; second, for the sake of giving rise to faith and understanding; third, for the sake of entering into the profound meaning;
fourth, for the sake of non-retrogression; fifth, for the sake of generating joy;
and sixth, for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma. This sutra is specifically intended to sever doubt, so that those who have doubts may attain their severance. For this reason...
It is for the sake of immature bodhisattvas so that they may develop faith and understanding in the *prajñā* upon hearing of its great merit;
for mature bodhisattvas so that they may enter into its profound meaning; for those who have already attained freedom from contempt so that their diligent minds may no longer regress;
and for those who have already attained a pure mind so that they may experience joy. It is also to enable the Mahāyāna teaching to endure in future ages.
Because he has dwelled [in this practice] for a long time, it is for these reasons that Śūnyatānirdeśa asks the question. "How should one dwell?
refers to aspiration and vow. "Subduing the mind" refers to the suppression of distraction. Within this context, "aspiration" means the correct seeking.

"Vow" (*praṇidhāna*) means to form a mental aspiration for the sake of what is sought. "Subduing distraction" means that if the mind of *samāpatti* becomes scattered, one restrains it and causes it to abide once more.
Question: In other translations, after the phrase "how to abide," there is an additional line:
"how to practice. Why is this absent in this translation? Answer: This is because the profound Dharma of Prajñā is the fruit of the Buddha’s [realization].

Abiding. A Bodhisattva who wishes to abide in this [state] gives rise to a great vow. Since it is known that once the mind has been awakened, one must necessarily initiate practice, the meaning of abiding is fully contained herein;
therefore, it is treated briefly. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s Seal of Approval.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said: the Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Sons and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this manner and subdue themselves in this manner."
Regarding the phrase "Excellent, your mind": the treatise states that because the question was excellent, one should address the Elder Subhūti as "Excellent.
Thus, while the practices of the three vehicles differ, this question pertains solely to the bodhisattva; as it accords with the Buddha-mind, the question is indeed excellent. Great!
The Treatise says: "Subhūti, he delights in practicing the samādhi of non-contention and constantly maintains compassion for sentient beings.

Although he cannot extensively deliver sentient beings, he always assists the Bodhisattvas by inquiring about their affairs. That the Buddha spoke 'Excellent! Excellent! a second time was for this reason."
This is the ultimate excellence. "Now listen attentively," and so forth, means that wishing to respond to his request, [the Buddha] truly commands him to listen attentively:
"You should abide in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, and subdue your mind in this way; I shall now proclaim this for you.
△ Third, Subhūti’s wish to hear.
"Yes, indeed. World-Honored One, we wish most earnestly to hear it.
"Yes, indeed" (*vande*) is a term of salutation and response. Master Xie said: "Having been granted permission through compassionate instruction, I now incline my heart with reverent solemnity.
△ Third, the places where the practices are established. From this point, the text is divided into eighteen dwellings (*vihāra*). First, the general outline shall be presented.

Next, the commentary is provided section by section. First, a general presentation of the overall framework has two parts: first, the listing of the chapters; second, the determination of the stages. Regarding the first, the listing of the chapters: 1.
Initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*); 2. Practice; 3. Desire to obtain the dwelling place of the form body (*rūpakāya*); 4.

Desire to obtain the dwelling place of the dharma body (*dharmakāya*); 5. Cultivating the path to attain excellence without pride; 6. Appearing in the world for the sake of not being separated from the Buddha.
At that time: (1) purifying the Buddha-field through seven vows; (2) maturing sentient beings; (3) remaining far removed from the distractions of conforming to external treatises;
(4) contemplating the disintegration of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); (5) making offerings to the Tathāgata; (6) remaining far removed from indolence;
(7) clarifying patience (*kṣānti*); (8) being in accord with the Dharma; and (9) remaining far removed from joy at the time of realizing the path.
Movement. Sixteenth is seeking instruction; seventeenth is for the realization of the Path; eighteenth is seeking the Buddha-way above.
In the treatise, these are again collectively categorized as eight abodes at one time. Therefore, the treatise says: "Briefly, there are eight kinds, which are also sufficient.
First, the abode of inclusion; second, the pure abode of the pāramitās; third, the abode of desire; fourth, the abode of detachment..."
The dwelling place of hindrances; the fifth, the dwelling place of the pure mind; the sixth, the ultimate dwelling place; the seventh, the vast dwelling place;

and the eighth, the profound dwelling place. Furthermore, the "dwelling place of gathering" refers to the generation of the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), while the "dwelling place of purity" refers to spiritual practice (*pratipatti*);
these two are the causes. The desire to attain the result—the *rūpakāya* and *dharmakāya*—is the fruit. This provides a general demonstration of cause and effect. If one were to depart from this...
The "obstructions" comprise the twelve stages (*vihāra*); their specific characteristics are the cause. The "ultimate purity of mind" is the realization of the Buddha-way;
this is the fruit. The remaining two [categories] span the entire sūtra horizontally, manifesting the vastness and profundity of Prajñā.
Thus, one should know that the eighteen [dharmas] are subsumed within the eight stages in order to demonstrate the relationship between the general and the particular.
This is merely the meaning of the two-fold cause and effect. △ Second, the determination of stages (*bhūmi*).

The sequential order of the arising of these eighteen abodes (*vihāra*) will be explained and demonstrated according to the text; it is not presented here in advance to avoid prolixity. As for the determination of the stages:

indeed, the eighteen abodes are themselves the stages, in the sense of being that which is relied upon. Why, then, should they be further analyzed and explained by way of the [standard] stages? It should be...

It is known that the eighteen stages of the dwelling-practice positions (*vihāra*) all collectively receive the name "dwelling. The reason they are specifically analyzed and explained by way of three distinct grounds is as follows:
the first sixteen dwellings, wherein ignorance has not yet been destroyed, are collectively designated as the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*).
The seventeenth, wherein ignorance is destroyed and one enters the path of realization, is named the ground of pure mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*). The eighteenth is the upward-seeking [stage].
The Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) is precisely the Tathāgata-ground. This is the general and concise meaning of the Sūtra.

The Treatise (*śāstra*) establishes a threefold classification of grounds, which encompasses both the *bie* (separate) and *yuan* (perfect) teachings; there is no need to further correlate these with other systems of stages.

However, regarding the fifteenth stage, the time of realizing the Path (*mārga*), where one is far removed from the movement of joy, and the seventeenth stage, the dwelling place of realizing the Path—how do they differ? The answer, as stated in the Commentary (*vṛtti*), is:

This sutra encompasses both teachings. At first glance, the text appears to refer exclusively to the distinct (pratyekabuddha) stage, because it generally designates those prior to the [Bodhisattva] grounds as being in the "stage of faith-practice" (*śraddhā-caryā*).

If one were to interpret this according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanwei*), then even the realization of the Path at the First Abode (*prathamābhūmi*) would still be termed the "stage of faith-practice," as in the *Awakening of Faith*, which explains that the First Abode of Initial Resolve is called the "resolve accomplished through faith. However, I maintain that this is not the case, for it contradicts the treatise.
This is incorrect. First, the treatise itself states: "At the time of realizing the Way (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*), one remains far removed from the movement of joy (*prīti-īraṇā*).

Thus, as one is about to enter the realization of the Way, there is a fear that the mind will give rise to the movement of joy; if one were to personally grasp at views (*dṛṣṭi*), this would obstruct the Way, and therefore it must be abandoned.

This indicates that one enters the realization of the Way precisely by being free from the movement of joy; it cannot yet be said that one has attained the perfect realization of the Way. Second, because...

The eight abodes: from the fifth, the stage of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), wherein one attains excellence and is free from pride, up to the sixteenth, wherein one seeks instruction—these twelve stages in total are subsumed within the eight abodes for dwelling free from obstacles.

The seventeenth is the stage of realization (sākṣātkriyāmārga), which is the eighth among them, the abode of the pure mind. Thus, by virtue of being free from obstacles, the mind becomes pure and enters the path of realization.
Furthermore, if one has not yet entered into realization, it is still merely a semblance of the Way; therefore, it is called the Stage of Practice through Faith (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*).

For this reason, we know that the fifteenth [stage] reveals the positions of the internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of both the Distinct and Complete Teachings, whereas the seventeenth stage, the Path of Realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*), is distinct from the semblance.
The sequence of the stages of practice is extremely clear in meaning; why do you persist in being ignorant? Question: Regarding the *prajñā* of the full letters (*pūrṇākṣara*).
[Question: It should apply to all three teachings. Why then does the treatise judge the stages as belonging only to the Separate and Perfect [Teachings]? [Answer: Jingxi said:

"Therefore, at the stage of the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*, only these two [the Separate and Perfect] are required. This clarifies the meaning of the "unshared" (exclusive) [teaching], which is the intention of the [Vaipulya] section.

Although the intention is unshared, there are still those who newly receive the Small Vehicle through the Expedient Gate; when they reach this point, they must be integrated. Furthermore, there are those who have incidentally attained the Small Vehicle through the Mahāyāna Gate; this is [the case].

Therefore, they are used concurrently. Thus we know that the *Śāstra*, according to the intent of its divisions (*bhu*), clarifies that the stages (*bhūmi*) exist only within the Separate and Perfect Teachings.

However, if one considers the inclusion of capacities (*indriya*) based on the Dharma, then the meaning extends through all three teachings. To verify the teaching by means of the stages is precisely what is illustrated in the passage below concerning the four fruits.
△ Second, the explanation of the text is divided into eighteen sections. Regarding the first, the arousal of the mind, there are two parts. First, the introduction of the person:
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner."

The Commentary states: "To briefly mention 'subduing' (vibhava) necessarily implies 'abiding' (sthitā). This is because the destruction [of afflictions] must invariably involve contemplating the principle (tattva).
Therefore, after explaining the practice below, it concludes: 'One should simply abide as instructed.
Here too, mentioning 'abiding' necessarily implies 'subduing,' because contemplating the principle is precisely what enables one to destroy delusions. In the Treatise, both abiding and subduing...
They are explained simultaneously. Therefore, the scriptural text employs elliptical expression by citing them alternately.
△ Second, showing the characteristics. As the verse says: "Vast, foremost, and eternal; its mind is non-erroneous; abiding in a profound mind of benefit;
the merits of this vehicle are fulfilled. According to this, the text is divided into four parts. First is the vast mind, which is "vast" because the mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
It is vast.
All categories of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
whether possessing form or formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception.
"All sentient beings" is the general enumeration; "womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born" are the specific characteristics.

The commentary explains that these are distinctions subsumed under the spheres of birth, dependence, and environment; yet, by means of these three categories, all sentient beings are collectively encompassed.

First, regarding birth: one is born according to karma, which consists of the four modes of birth (*yoni*). Although this principle applies generally to the aforementioned [realms], for the time being it refers specifically to the four miserable destinies (*durgati*), the four continents (*dvīpa*), and the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Second, regarding the basis of support: although this applies generally to the lower realms, for the time being it takes the meditative absorptions of the form and formless realms as its basis;
thus, the four dhyānas constitute the "with-form" (*rūpin*) and the sphere of infinite space constitutes the "formless" (*arūpin*). Third, regarding the objective field...

Regarding this, Qinglong says: "The objective sphere is cited to manifest the mind. Because mental perception (*saṃjñā*) is difficult to know, the objective sphere is cited to manifest that perception.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Based on the distinctions of the mind, three types of sentient beings are established: those with perception, those without perception, and those who are neither.

That is to say, the station of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) is 'with perception'; the station of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is 'without perception'; and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is 'neither'."
△ Second, the first thought [of enlightenment]:
"I shall cause all beings to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to final liberation.
Here, "I" refers to the one who has resolved their mind; it encompasses all sentient beings, including those born from wombs, eggs, and so forth, and brings them all into the great vow.
He brings them all to parinirvāṇa by means of the foremost and most excellent dharma, which is nirvana without remainder. This is indeed the fundamental responsibility of a bodhisattva.
Herein, the remedy is for those who do not resolve to attain enlightenment and do not deliver sentient beings—such individuals are practitioners of the heterodox path.
△ Third, the Mind of Constancy:
"In this way, I shall bring immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, yet in reality, there are no sentient beings who have attained parinirvāṇa.
This "bringing to parinirvāṇa" reiterates the first mind mentioned previously; "immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings" reiterates what was stated before.
The vast mind: "In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction. This clarifies that the great compassion of the Bodhisattva is of one essence.
He regards sentient beings as being just like his own body; when sentient beings attain liberation, it is as if he himself has attained liberation.
How could he perceive anyone as a recipient of deliverance? Therefore, it is said that "in truth, there are none. △ Fourth, the non-perverted mind.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of "other" toward all sentient beings, that notion is transformed and is no longer their own essence; for there would be [an object] to be perceived as other.
One who possesses [such views] maintains the duality of subject and object, and holds the discriminatory view of a self and persons; such a person is not a bodhisattva.
To examine this thoroughly, the treatise refutes the characteristics of a self, persons, and so forth. It states:

"In this context, grasping at one's own continuity as a self-characteristic, and sequentially grasping at other realms of existence as the characteristic of others, and grasping at what belongs to them as 'mine'..."
The mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*). From "self" up to "as long as life remains," one grasps these as the mark of life. The commentary states:

One grasps the internal aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the mark of self; one grasps other realms or non-humans as the mark of a human; one calculates the four aggregates belonging to "what belongs to me" (*ātmīya*) as continuing the preceding aggregate of consciousness;
and the combination of these five aggregates constitutes the mark of a sentient being. One calculates subsequent life-span as the mark of a life-possessor (*jīvaka-nimitta*). △

Second is the practice (*pratipatti*). For now, the previous section on the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) has already answered that question. Since one knows how to arouse the mind, one must necessarily engage in practice;
through practice, one fulfills one's vows. Therefore, the characteristics of practice are further demonstrated. The Sūtra says, "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*). Question:

From this point downward, the seventeen stages (*vihāra*) are all, in relation to the initial arousal of the mind, categorized as characteristics of practice. Why is only this [section] specifically designated as "practice"?

Yes. [The Master] replied: "One sutra elucidates the practice of the six *pāramitās*. Herein, by clarifying *dāna* (generosity), all six *pāramitās* are fully encompassed, thereby providing a general demonstration of the characteristics of the practices throughout the entire sutra;
hence it says 'cultivation. The *Shu* (Commentary) maintains that taking the meaning of *dāna* as the central theme accords perfectly with the intent of the treatise, and we shall follow this.
The text is divided into three parts: first, the clarification of generosity; second, the manifestation of merit; third..."
Exhortation to Rely on the Teaching. This section has two parts. First, the clarification of the mode of practice; second, the demonstration of avoiding faults. The first part also has two sections.
First, not dwelling upon future fruits.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling upon any phenomenon (*dharma*).

When a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi of correspondence and gathers the distracted mind, they practice the dharma of giving within the pāramitās and thereby realize that the three factors—the object, the giver, and the recipient—are empty in essence. Since there is nothing that is not the nature of the perfect and eternal Prajñā, what is there to dwell upon or cling to?
Therefore it is said: "One should practice giving by dwelling nowhere. Thus, all three [theories] are...
This is explained by way of the three kinds of giving. As the verse says: "The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) encompasses six: material goods, fearlessness, and the Dharma;

among these, one, two, and three are called the stages of practice. This refers to the inclusion of the dharmas. The "one" mentioned in the verse is because material goods include the single category of giving (*dāna*).
The "two" is because fearlessness includes both ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*). The "three" is because...

The gift of Dharma encompasses the three [perfections] of diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; therefore, it is referred to as "one, two, and three. First, the gift of material sustenance (*āmiṣadāna*):
one gives with an impartial mind, free from love or hatred. In this way, one is able to nourish and increase the retribution of merit;
hence it is called the gift of material sustenance. Second, the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*): by means of upholding the precepts, one eliminates stinginess and attachment.
With a mind that, according to whatever is requested, is able to give everything away to benefit sentient beings without any fear or timidity;

because of his patience, he has eliminated his own anger and practices loving-kindness and compassion, so that his mind is free from defilement and he can relinquish all things, just like the Rishi below—this is precisely what that refers to.
Regarding the third, the gift of Dharma: if one lacks diligence, toward those who receive the Dharma...

When preaching the Dharma to others, if one is weary, one will be unable to preach. If one lacks meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one will crave offerings of faith and respect, and being unable to endure the afflictions of cold and heat, one will preach with a defiled mind.
If one lacks wisdom (*prajñā*), one will preach erroneously and commit many transgressions. Without these three [qualities], one cannot accomplish the gift of the Dharma.

Question: If the *Yuanlun* (Treatise on the Perfect) maintains that the six perfections mutually encompass one another such that each perfection contains all six, why does this [text] speak only of giving (*dāna*) as encompassing the six?
Answer: That the six perfections mutually encompass one another is a statement concerning the level of principle (*li*). That giving encompasses the six is a statement concerning phenomena (*shi*).
Thus, by clarifying giving through the lens of phenomena, it demonstrates the practice of not dwelling in signs (*animitta*). As the treatise says: "Those various waves... [and so forth].
The *pāramitās* have two kinds of fruits: namely, those of the future and those of the present. Regarding the fruits of the future: through *dāna*, one obtains great rewards of merit;
through *śīla*, one obtains a perfect physical form, such as that of Śakra or Brahmā; through *kṣānti*, one obtains great assistance and a vast retinue;
through *vīrya*, one obtains uninterrupted continuity of rewards and so forth; and through *dhyāna*, one obtains a birth-body that is not...
It may be impaired. Through *prajñā*, one attains sharp and keen faculties as well as various forms of joy. Among the great assembly, one attains mastery and so forth.

If bodhisattvas practice giving for the sake of seeking future fruits and dwell upon it—engaging in the act of giving like a flower that anticipates its fruit—then their mind dwells on signs (*nimitta*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Regarding phenomena (*dharma*), one should have nothing to which one clings."
One dwells and practices in giving. △ Second, not dwelling in present fruits:
that is to say, not dwelling in form when practicing giving; not dwelling in sound, odor, taste, touch, or dharmas when practicing giving.

The Treatise says: "If one seeks results in the present life, one practices giving out of faith, reverence, and devotion; one practices giving for the sake of abiding in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
If one practices giving for the sake of attaining *nirvāṇa* in the present life, one practices giving for the sake of abiding in the Dharma.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'One should practice giving without abiding in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. The Treatise says: 'To practice giving without abiding' means..."
This very non-abiding is for the purpose of establishing the ultimate truth. △ Second, demonstrating the freedom from faults:
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner, not abiding in signs.
The Treatise says: This is for the purpose of revealing what is called "corresponding samādhi" and the "gathering of the distracted mind.
Regarding these two periods—present and future—if one does not dwell upon the perception of marks, then one dwells neither in the existence of marks nor in the absence of marks.
Because one abides in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence. △ Second, the revelation of merit. This also has two parts; first, merit...
It is immeasurable. Why?
If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, their merit and virtue cannot be measured or conceived.
The Treatise says: Having thus established non-dwelling, there may be some bodhisattvas who, out of a craving for merit and virtue, [regard] this...
It is unbearable. In order to make it bearable, the World-Honored One reveals that practicing giving without abiding produces merit so vast it is inconceivable.
II. Comparing it to the Great Void.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space of the eastern direction be measured? No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured? No, World-Honored One."
Subhūti, the merit of a bodhisattva’s giving that is without abiding in signs is likewise such that it cannot be measured or conceived.
The Treatise says: It is like empty space, for three reasons: first, it pervades all places, because merit arises within both the state of abiding and the state of non-abiding;
second, it is vast and expansive, being lofty, great, and preeminent; third, it is inexhaustible, reaching to the ultimate end.
Because it is inexhaustible. By this, one may compare it to the merit of Prajñāpāramitā: because its nature pervades the *dharmadhātu*, it is like the great void pervading all things.
Because it is loftier and more sublime than the three vehicles which are partial and narrow, it is like the void being high, vast, and preeminent.
Because it can lead to the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi, it is like the void being infinite and ultimate. △ Three: Exhortation.
"Subhūti, in accordance with this teaching, a bodhisattva should dwell only as thus taught.
△ Third, regarding the dwelling place for those who wish to attain the form-body (rūpakāya), there are three parts. First, the question.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks?

This question is posed from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The two preceding chapters were spoken by the Buddha himself to demonstrate the cultivation of the resolve for awakening (*bodhicitta*).
This is the cause. A cause must necessarily yield its fruit. One might suppose that the Tathāgata, by means of cultivation as the cause, attained this physical form upon reaching the fruit.
To prevent such a misconception—that one can perceive the accomplishment of this material body through seeing—it is for this reason that he asks the question. △ Second, the answer.
"No, World-Honored One. One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not physical marks."
He answered by means of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The Tathāgata’s form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) exists in dependence upon conditions and is therefore not ultimate.

He replied, "No. Thus, one cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of the marks of the form-body; rather, the bodily marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are precisely the signless Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
This refers to the fact that the response-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) is itself the Dharma-body. "This body of mine now... [is it?]
This is precisely the Dharma-body. △ Third, the conclusion:
The Buddha told Subhūti, "Whatever marks there may be are all false and illusory. If one perceives that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata."
The Treatise states: This reveals the establishment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Within this, the accomplishment of marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is false;
the non-accomplishment of marks is not false. The accomplishment of the thirty-two marks—these secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) are not real;
they are all false. As for the non-accomplishment of marks: "If one sees that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata"—this is not false.
The Commentary states: "The two dharmas of defilement and purity consist of both general and specific delusions and belong to the category of the illusory.
Since it is said that 'all marks whatsoever are entirely illusory,' how can one differentiate between divergent interpretations? This clarifies the marks of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body);

how could one employ the two delusions of defilement and purity to explain them? Question: Regarding the dwelling place of the *rūpakāya* (form-body), why is it pointed out that the response-body is itself the Dharma-body, and that marks are themselves non-marks?
If that is so, does this not manifest the Dharma-body? Answer: The Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) and the Dharma-body are of one essence and mutually identical.

However, by merely eliminating false conceptualization (parikalpita), one must understand that this does not mean setting aside the characteristics of the Reward-body to point exclusively to the Dharma-body and call it "non-characteristic.
△ Fourth, regarding the dwelling place of the Dharma-body, there are two parts: first, the Dharma-body as taught in the scriptures; second, its realization.
The Dharma-body. The first section also has two parts. First, the question:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases as these..."
Do you give rise to true faith?

Because one practices after generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one reaches the stage of the fruition where the physical marks are perfected; hearing this directly from the Buddha makes it easy to believe and understand.

However, sentient beings in the末法 (final dharma) age have shallow spiritual faculties, and I truly fear that for them, belief and understanding will be even more difficult upon hearing this. Therefore, [the teaching] relies on external objects to bring it forth.
Question: Therefore it is said, "Are there any sentient beings, etc., who hear these phrases? The *Śāstra* states:

Regarding the seven kinds of meanings and phrases that have been explained, having a perception of their meaning as non-perverted is called true faith. One should know that to grasp at the meaning according to the literal words is not true faith.
This is because true faith is difficult to obtain; for this reason, the question is asked. II. The Answer. This is in five parts. First:
This demonstrates the practice.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not speak thus. After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit, who will be able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses, regarding them as true."
"Do not speak thus" is a negation of what was asked; it means that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there will indeed be those capable of generating such faith.
Regarding "the final five hundred years," the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* lists them directly as follows: in the first hundred years, liberation is firm;
in the second hundred years, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is firm; in the third hundred years, the precepts (*śīla*) are maintained... [text continues].
In the fourth century, the firmness of ethical discipline (*śīla*) will predominate; in the fifth century, the firmness of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).
There are five periods of five hundred years within the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*. From the first to the fourth, the matters are identical to those in the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*;
only in the fifth is it said that "strife and contention" (*raṇa*) will be firm. Thus, one should know that the present text takes the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* as authoritative, as translated by Yijing.
The original text states: "In the future age, at the time when the True Dharma is extinguished," and so forth. The "time when the True Dharma is extinguished" refers to the final five hundred years.

The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If, in the final age during the last five hundred years when the True Dharma is extinguished, the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the upholder of the Dharma—these three—are not present.
Here, the "upholder of the Dharma" refers to the Sangha Jewel; thus, these are the three.
When the Dharma-treasure has vanished, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit. Merit is the initial gateway to the six perfections;

the precepts are the foundation of meditative concentration and wisdom. Thus, after the extinction [of the Buddha], those who possess and maintain such merit can receive the Way and give rise to faith.
II. Revealing the Causes for Accumulation.
It should be known that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;

rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable tens of millions of Buddhas. Upon hearing these phrases, even for a single thought-moment, they give rise to pure faith.

Since the planting of the Buddha-seeds is manifold, the manifestation of deep-rooted roots of goodness indicates that the accumulated causes are supreme. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Subhūti asks the Buddha:
"Who is able to believe and understand this profound Prajñā? The Buddha replies: "There are bodhisattvas who, in the presence of previous Buddhas, have long cultivated the six perfections;
their roots of goodness are matured, and they have made offerings to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas."
The Buddha said, "One who constantly associates with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) is able to have faith.

Subhūti asked again, "What are the characteristics and what are the signs of one who has faith in the Prajñāpāramitā? The Buddha said, "The severance and departure from desire, anger, and delusion are the marks of such faith.
Furthermore, the severance of desire, anger, and delusion is the subduing of distraction; this is truly because one abides in the characteristic of this Prajñāpāramitā."
When one enters samādhi, one is able to subdue distraction; abiding in prajñā is called the arising of faith.
Even the arising of pure faith for a single moment involves believing in the marks and signs that adorn the body of the fruit, all of which arise from a mind of non-apprehension.
