And thus accomplishment is attained. The treatise says: "This demonstrates the cause of accumulation.
If even a single mind of pure faith can yield such merit and virtue, how much more so when one gives rise to the true mark [of reality]? △ Third, demonstrating being embraced by a virtuous friend.
"Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees all these sentient beings.
Vasubandhu says: "It is sufficient to know that the Tathāgata fully knows; for what reason does he further say 'fully sees'?

If he did not say 'fully sees,' one might think that the Tathāgata knows them through inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*). Fearing that such a thought might arise, [he says this]. If that were so, then..."
It is said that the Tathāgata sees all. Why, then, is it further said that he knows all?
If "knows all" were not stated, one might think that the Tathāgata sees with the fleshly eye and so forth. To prevent such a thought, both terms are necessary. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"By speaking of both 'knowing' and 'seeing,' the matter becomes firm; it is like a rope that becomes strong when two strands are joined as one. Furthermore, regarding knowing and seeing:
What is this? The treatise says: "The knower knows the name-body; the seer sees the form-body.
This means that throughout all activities of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, one knows the mind and perceives its basis, which is in accord with *prajñā*.
Therefore, it is encompassed by this [result]. △ Fourth, the manifestation of correspondence with merit.
One obtains such immeasurable merit.
According to the translation, it says: "one generates such immeasurable merit" or "one takes up such immeasurable merit. The *Śāstra* states:
"Generates" refers to the time when the merit is actually arising; "takes up" refers to the time of its cessation, because at that moment one retains the seeds.
One must know that birth is the cause of accumulation (*saṃbhava-hetu*). When this cause of accumulation ceases, it sustains the seeds of the virtuous essence along with the causal conditions;
thus, it corresponds with merit. This sutra merely says "attainment" and does not mention the "cause," because the cause of accumulation has already been explained previously.
△ Fifth, the manifestation of true perception (*bhūta-saṃjñā*) is divided into three parts. First, true perception is free from delusion.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span;
they have no notion of phenomena, nor do they have any notion of non-phenomena.
The *Śāstra* says: "To manifest the perception of reality (*bhūta-saṃjñā*) is the antidote to false grasping (*mithyā-grāha*). 'Perception' (*saṃjñā*) refers to mental perception.

If the mind grasps at phenomena as either 'dharma' or 'adharma,' then it is not the perception of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). The *Commentary* (*Vyākhyā*) says: "Regarding 'dharma' and 'adharma,' there are many ways of explaining them.

As explained by the Venerable Zhiyi: 'Dharma' refers to phenomena that are wholesome or unwholesome, and those that are provisional or real. 'Adharma' refers to that which lacks both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and the provisional..."

This is the reality of phenomena. Therefore, one knows that the characteristics of existence and non-existence are precisely the two truths: the ultimate and the conventional. Now, I say this is not so.

The sutra clearly states that there is neither dharma nor non-dharma; this is intended to abandon attachment. Thus, it abandons attachment to the two extremes of existence and non-existence, and one should not interpret its meaning as the two truths.
Moreover, the interpretation offered by the Wise One himself relies on the dualistic views of existence and non-existence.

Explaining what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, I shall now set forth the texts in their entirety to refute such errors, while still following my own interpretation. Thus, the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) states:
"Dharma consists merely of the two minds of good and evil, as well as the conventional and ultimate dharmas. If one perceives the existence of good and evil as mere provisional names..."
Furthermore, to perceive the real dharmas of good and evil is precisely to be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
What is called the "mark of non-dharmas" refers to the non-existence of the provisional names of good and evil, as well as the non-existence of the real dharmas of good and evil;

to perceive these is likewise to be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. Why is this? Because one gives rise to views based upon non-existence. (Full text) Therefore, we know that... [The Great...]
The Master distinguishes two views to explain what is dharma and what is non-dharma, clarifying them as clearly as the sun. Why then speak of the "two truths"?
As for what is called good and evil, this is generally categorized according to the arising of the mind in relation to the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) and the six obscurations (ṣaḍāvaraṇa).

If one perceives a distinction between good and evil within the obscurations and the perfections, this is attachment to provisional names (prajñapti). If one perceives that the obscurations and the perfections evoke retributions of good and evil, this is attachment to substantial dharmas (dravyadharma).

Therefore, to perceive these as provisional names and real dharmas is called the characteristic of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). If one perceives them as non-existent, thereby repudiating cause and effect, it is called the non-characteristic of dharmas (*adharmalakṣaṇa*).
△ Second, the re-explanation and exhortation to abandon [these views].
Why is this? If these sentient beings grasp at signs with their minds, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
If they grasp at the signs of dharmas, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Why is this? If they grasp at the signs of non-dharmas...
This constitutes clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas.

If the mind grasps at signs, this is a re-explanation that confirms the preceding point. As the previous text stated, "These sentient beings no longer have the notion of a self," etc., it is because the mind abides in the perception of reality and does not grasp at signs that they do not exist; conversely, this implies that if the mind were to grasp at [signs], [they would arise].

To perceive characteristics (*nimitta*) is itself to be attached to the notions of self (*ātman*), person (*pudgala*), and so forth. If one grasps at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it results in the aforementioned "non-existence of the characteristic of phenomena" (*adharmalakṣaṇa*).

This serves as a reductio ad absurdum to show that if one grasps at the characteristics of phenomena, one is immediately attached to the notions of self, person, and so forth. Why is this? [This] interrogates and explains:

since grasping at the characteristics of phenomena already constitutes attachment to the notions of self, person, and so forth, if one were to grasp at the characteristics of non-phenomena (*adharmalakṣaṇa*), one would likewise be attached to the notions of self, person, and so forth. Yet, for what reason is this further [the case]?
There is the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). It should be understood that this is due to the non-abandonment of ignorance (*avidyā*). The treatise states:
"However, because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the notion of a self are not abandoned, there is the latent ignorance associated with the grasping at a self and so forth.

Question: What is the difference between the terms *ze* (則) and *ji* (即) used here? Answer: Although both are particles, each has its own specific meaning. *Ze* (則) functions as a particle of citation.
The word "above" (shàng) is a term used to generally prohibit the arising of the mind; if one gives rise to such a mind, it constitutes the production of attachment.

The word "that" (jí) is a term that points to phenomena (dharmas); it serves to demonstrate the fault of giving rise to such a mind. If one gives rise to a mind that grasps at the characteristics of dharmas or the characteristics of non-dharmas, this is identical to the dualistic reckoning of existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is called "immediately attached" (jí zhù). "Immediately" (jí) means "at once" (shì). "Is" (shì) [refers to the state of being thus].
"Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas," and so forth. One who abides in *prajñā* should remain free from conceptual discrimination; thus it says "should not.
This exhorts the abandonment of a mind of attachment. △ Third, the conclusion by means of an analogy.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said: "O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the simile of the raft.
Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not Dharma."
Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata constantly says," this refers to the *Raft Simile Sūtra* (*Kullūpama-sutta*) from the *Āgamas*. That sūtra states: "The Buddha said:

'I have taught the parable of the raft; even these dharmas must be abandoned, let alone those that are not dharmas. The present text borrows the meaning of that metaphor to conclude and clarify that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is without grasping.
Here, "dharmas" refers to both provisional and ultimate dharmas, while "non-dharmas" refers to that which is neither provisional nor ultimate.
The Dharma. Thus, when the teaching speaks of cause and effect, if one gives rise to fixed attachment, this attachment becomes a view;
even this should be abandoned, let alone the denial of cause and effect, for such a position is logically untenable. How could one not abandon it? Therefore it is said:

"Even the Dharma should be abandoned, how much more so that which is non-Dharma. The Treatise says: "This demonstrates that a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the Dharma-body of speech should not [cling to]..."

The perception of unreality: regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and non-phenomena (*adharma*), this is precisely the perception of unreality. The commentary states: "The force of the phrasing in this passage is no different from what preceded it;
however, the interpretation of the meaning cannot be treated as a single uniform rule. Previously, conventional truth was taken as 'phenomenon' and ultimate truth as 'non-phenomenon'."
In this context, one might argue that what is practiced by the four types of noble ones constitutes the Dharma, while what is practiced by the six classes of ordinary beings constitutes non-Dharma;

however, this is not so. This is because such an interpretation fails to resolve the preceding errors regarding Dharma and non-Dharma, and consequently, it produces a divergent explanation that renders the meaning of the text incoherent.
△ Second, the realization of the Dharmakāya. Now, although the Dharmakāya is fundamentally...

There is. To realize [this] necessarily depends upon the adornment of merit and wisdom. Now, following that which adorns, the text is divided into two parts: first, the Dharma-body of the aspect of wisdom;
second, the Dharma-body of the aspect of merit. The first part is further divided into two: first, the question.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma?
If Subhūti were to answer this question in such a manner, the World-Honored One would have something to be attained, thereby following his own biased views.
If he says "no," then it is evident that the Tathāgata has indeed attained the fruit of Bodhi and preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
It was for this specific purpose that He posed this question: His intention was to see how Subhūti would comprehend what the Buddha had realized. II. The Answer. This has three parts. First:
"One does not grasp at the signs of what should be taught as realization.
Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can teach."

As for the statement that there is no fixed dharma: the Elder Subhūti, following the Buddha’s intention and according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), asserts that there is both awakening (*bodhi*) and attainment.
This is because they are sustained by aspiration and desire; through skillful means (*upāya*), both are existent.
If one follows the intention of the World-Honored One’s teaching, both [the teacher and the listener] are non-existent. To clarify this, the Sūtra states:
"As I understand the meaning of what the World-Honored One has taught," and so forth. Thus, it is known that emptiness gives rise to the understanding of the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching.

Therefore, he answers by means of the *dharmakāya* of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), rather than relying on the *nirmāṇakāya* of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). This is because the *nirmāṇakāya* manifests according to conditions and lacks [independent] existence.
Because it is definitively real. As the verse says: "The manifested and transformational [bodies] are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma.

Second, the correct manifestation that the Dharmakāya is without grasping. Why is this? All teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are neither graspable nor expressible; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
The treatise states: Because one attains bodhi by means of teaching the Dharma, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is established within the teaching of the Dharma.

Within this, there is nothing to be grasped; that is to say, when the listener correctly hears it, there is nothing to be spoken of, because when the speaker expounds it, they rely upon the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
Thus, there is neither grasping nor speaking. It is not a phenomenon (*dharma*), meaning it is not the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
It is not that it is non-dharmic; for within that *tathatā* (suchness), the characteristic of *anātman* (non-self) exists.
Thus, since the teaching of the Dharma is thus, one attains *bodhi*. By this principle, it should be known that the Sūtra uses the word "all" (*sarva*) as a term of inclusion.
△ Third, the sages and saints equally realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Why is this so? Because all worthy sages (ārya) are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The *Śāstra* says: "Because they are unconditioned, they are named 'sages' (*ārya*). To be unconditioned means to be free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).
If this is so, how can there be any distinction? One should know that while the unconditioned is like space, birds in flight have their heights and depths. Thus says the *Śāstra*.
There are two kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding the first unconditioned: it pertains to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

In terms of cultivation, it corresponds to *samāpatti* (meditative attainment) and occurs at the time of subduing distraction; thus, its meaning encompasses both the real and the semblance. This is designated as the "unconditioned" of a bodhisattva in training (*śaikṣa*).
Regarding the second unconditioned: it pertains solely to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It is the final cessation of cultivation because it is unsurpassed awakening. This is...
The Tathāgata is designated by the name "One Beyond Training" (aśaikṣa). Therefore, it is said that there are distinctions based on unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
From this point onward, throughout all the stages of abiding, it is clearly shown that one is designated as a "Noble One" (*ārya*) precisely because of the unconditioned.

It should be understood that in the preceding stages of abiding, it was not yet stated that the name is derived from the unconditioned. II. The Dharmakāya of Meritorious Characteristics. The text is divided as follows:
Two. First, the comparison of merit; second, the revelation of the reason. The first [section] has two parts: first, showing that the merit of giving jewels is great;
second, revealing that the merit of upholding this sutra is superior. The first [of these two] also has two parts: first, the question.
Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great?
The treatise states: "Regarding the giving of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system as the seven treasures, etc., how is this demonstrated?
It is precisely that which is called the *dharmakāya* of verbal teaching which gives birth to the auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata’s merit.

The attainment of the *dharmakāya* truly arises from the guidance of *prajñā*, through the combined practice of phenomena and principle, which is able to produce the *dharmakāya* of auspicious marks. As for the "three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system," [it is defined] in the *Abhidharmakośa*...
The verse says: One thousand sets of the four great continents, suns and moons, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds, is called a small chiliocosm.
(One set of four continents, one sun and moon, one Mount Sumeru, up to one set of the six heavens of the desire realm and one heaven of the first dhyāna, is called one world.

One thousand such worlds, all covered by a single heaven of the second dhyāna, is called a small chiliocosm. One thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm. (Furthermore, one thousand small chiliocosms is called a medium chiliocosm.)

Within that interval, there are a total of one billion first dhyānas and one thousand second dhyānas, all of which are subsumed under the third dhyāna; this [system] multiplied by one thousand is a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*). Furthermore, one thousand medium chiliocosms is called a great trichiliocosm.

Within this interval, there are a total of ten trillion first dhyāna heavens, one billion second dhyāna heavens, and one thousand third dhyāna heavens, all of which are covered by the fourth dhyāna. They all share the same process of formation and destruction. [The world] is formed by the four wheels and destroyed by the three calamities:

fire reaches the first dhyāna, water reaches the second dhyāna, and wind reaches the third dhyāna. As for the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, and red pearls (and so forth). △ Second, the answer.
Subhūti said, “It is very much so, World-Honored One. Why is this? This merit is not the nature of merit;
therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.”
The Commentary states: "This is merit" refers to the merit of phenomena (*dharma*). "That which is not the nature of merit" means that the merit of phenomena is fundamentally empty.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata says that the merit is great, although it is empty, it is provisional. This explanation is incorrect.
If it is said that phenomena are fundamentally empty, then since emptiness lacks the four natures, one should not say "it is not.
Now, as for what is called "merit," this refers to the characteristic of merit within the Tathāgata’s two kinds of adornment. That which is "not the nature of merit" is discussed in the *Treatise*.
It says: "This negates the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*), because that accumulation of merit lacks an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) as a conceptualized entity.

It reveals that Prajñāpāramitā sweeps away all marks, being empty and devoid of an inherent nature as an accumulation of merit. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of 'much merit' [in order to negate the extreme of denial]."

The treatise states: This refutes the extreme of denial (*apavāda*). That [the Tathāgata] does not possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) according to his words, yet there is a thing that can be spoken of;
for the Tathāgata says that merit is great. Although there are no words, it is by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that the Tathāgata says merit is great.
Thus, he is free from the faults of the two extremes of increase and decrease, manifesting abiding in the Middle Way. Therefore, the treatise says: "By means of..."
This accumulation of merit encompasses the Dharma-body characterized by merit. Because it is guided and led by Prajñā, one thereby encompasses the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body characterized by merit;
thus, the superiority of the merit of this sutra is revealed. It is for this reason that the following comparison is made. This is what is meant.
△ Second, manifesting the superiority of the merit of upholding this sutra:
If there should be another person who, from within this sutra, receives and upholds even as little as a four-line verse, and explains it for others.
The merit of this is superior to that.
The Treatise states: "Even to speak a single four-line verse produces vast merit; how much more so the meritorious marks of the Tathāgata, culminating in the attainment of the Dharma-body.
The Treatise further states: "Regarding 'its merit,' this is spoken as a description of its characteristics, manifesting the nature of its merit."

Regarding the phrase "because it is the Dharma-body" and "that which excels it": this demonstrates that it is sustained by aspiration and resolve. Furthermore, it says: "Because it counteracts the non-arising of merit.
This means that the merit of material deeds (*vastu-puṇya*) cannot give rise to the Dharma-body, which is the characteristic of merit.

A verse states: "Merit does not lead to Bodhi; two things can lead to Bodhi. Material merit yields only a temporary reward of celestial bliss; once that merit is exhausted, it is fundamentally suffering."

The cause: not merely seeking enlightenment for oneself, but personally upholding [the Dharma] and expounding it for others—these two constitute the *prajñā* as the "cause of realization" (*yō-in*), which is capable of leading one to enlightenment.
Regarding the "four-line verse," the *Ekottarika-āgama-saṃgraha* states: "It refers to any essential verse cited from the sūtras, such as those concerning the Four Noble Truths.
The commentary (*sho*) states: "As for those that merely explain what accords with the Seal of the True Reality (*shinjitsu-sō-in*), they are extremely few."
Regarding the single phrase of the title: receiving, upholding, and explaining it, the merit obtained is in every way superior; this is merely cited by way of illustration using four phrases.

As for the "Seal of the True Reality" (*bhūtatathatā-mudrā*), as the *Zhìzhě* (Jizang) said: "This seal of the Great and Small [Vehicles] stamps the sutras of the Half-[Vehicle] and the Full-[Vehicle], such that external paths cannot intermingle with them and celestial Māras cannot destroy them.
It is like a worldly official document; when it bears the seal, it is trustworthy. Śāriputra said: "In the world..."
The World-Honored One has taught the true path; Pāpīyān possesses no such thing. The *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"If the various sūtras of the Hīnayāna are sealed with the three seals—impermanence, non-self, and nirvāṇa—know them to be the Buddha’s teaching; by practicing them, one attains the Way.

If they lack these three dharma-seals, they are the teachings of Māra. In the Mahāyāna, there is but a single dharma-seal, namely, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. This is called [the seal].
A definitive sutra (*nītārtha-sūtra*) that can lead one to attain the Great Way, yet lacks the Seal of the True Nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-mudrā*), is merely the teaching of Māra.

Now, when the Mahayana and Hinayana discuss the "Seal," they generally distinguish between the Great and the Small based on their respective categories: the sūtras of the Śrāvakas are the Small, while the various Mahayana sūtras are the Great.
Within the Mahayana category, although there are both the Universal (*sāmānya*) and Distinct (*viśeṣa*) teachings, these two do not constitute separate scriptural collections (*piṭaka*).
Thus, one adopts the superior teaching of the Master of the Section. It speaks solely of the single seal (*ekamudrā*) within the context of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). (And so forth. Question:
Ānanda, when the Buddha was on the verge of *parinirvāṇa*, he was outside the Śāla grove and was harassed by sixty-four trillion demons (*māra*).

These demons transformed themselves into the likeness of the Tathāgata, and so on, until they were able to preach the twelve divisions of the sūtras (*dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana*) and the thirty [dharmas] of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
There are seven categories [of teachings]. They simply cannot expound the Dharma-gate of the Perfect and Sudden, because the Perfect and Sudden is not within their realm.
Thus, since they have already expounded the Dharma-gates that revert to the Separate Teaching, there is no need to provide further explanation or validation;

why then say that external paths cannot intermingle with them or that Māras cannot destroy them? Answer: Although Māras may preach the twelve divisions of the scriptures, they possess no internal realization.
What is thus spoken lacks any definitive expression; how could those who hear it possibly attain the Way? Therefore, Miaoli said:
"Although Māra does not realize the distinct emptiness and the provisional, he is able to speak of distinct emptiness and the provisional. Because Māra does not realize them, he speaks erroneously;
there are only his words, but within the words there is no underlying meaning. If this is so, why did Ānanda not recognize it? As Jingxi said:

Because Ānanda lacked the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and because Māra had entered his very bones, although he recognized this was Māra, whenever he wished to rise or speak, his will was entirely thwarted.
II. Displaying the Reason for This. This is divided into two parts. First, displaying the supreme dignity of the sutra.
Why is this? Subhūti, all Buddhas and the Dharma of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas—all emerge from this sūtra.
The treatise asks: "By what causes and conditions can the recitation of even a single four-line verse within the *dharmakāya* of spoken teachings produce such great merit?
To establish this meaning, the Sūtra states that all Buddhas and the qualities of enlightenment (*bodhidharma*) are born from this;
therefore, one should know that Prajñā is named the Mother of the Buddhas. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The Buddha arises from Prajñā."

In the midst [of practice], one attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) as well as the body endowed with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*). △ Second, the negation of characteristics according to principle:
Subhūti, that which is called "Buddha-dharma" is precisely not Buddha-dharma.
The Treatise says: "From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one speaks of the Buddha’s birth because there is *bodhi*.
Because these two coexist, they are called the Buddha-dharma; yet, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), because of both *bodhi* and the Buddha, it is not the Buddha-dharma.
△ Fifth, regarding being free from pride when attaining excellence through the cultivation of the path, the Treatise says: "As previously briefly explained, there are eight types of abodes."
The following twelve [stages] are collectively termed the "remedies for dwelling free from obstacles.
Thus, one should know that throughout these twelve, there are always afflictive obstacles to be abandoned and corresponding remedies. Herein, it is for the purpose of abandoning pride (*māna*).

By attaining excellence through the path of cultivation, one practices the path of *prajñā* and thereby attains the four superior fruits. When pride is absent, one does not perceive anything as being attained. Question:
The preceding text has already clarified all noble ones (*ārya*). Why, then, is there a further discussion here regarding the four fruits (*phala*)? Answer:

The preceding text was intended to clarify that noble ones equally realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); here, it is because within these unconditioned dharmas, one attains that which is non-attainment. Question:

In the Sūtras, among the four fruits, why are the first three called "fruits" (*phala*), while the fourth is called the "path" (*mārga*)? Answer: [The answer follows: Because the first three fruits are the results of cultivation, they are designated as "fruits"; whereas the fourth fruit is the realization of the path itself, and thus it is designated as the "path. Furthermore, the first three fruits involve the exhaustion of defilements through the abandonment of fetters, and thus they are termed "fruits"; the fourth fruit, however, is the finality of the path where no further cultivation remains, and thus it is termed the "path. Finally, the first three fruits are states of fruition resulting from the path, hence they are called "fruits," while the fourth fruit is the ultimate state of the path’s completion, and thus it is called the "path. Therefore, the distinction between calling the first three "fruits" and the fourth "the path" is established.

Regarding the first three fruits: in terms of the names of their opposites, and within the scope of the divisions of abandonment and realization, they are spoken of by pairing the Chinese and Sanskrit terms for the sake of conveniently manifesting the meaning of non-apprehension. As for the fourth fruit, there is no corresponding [Sanskrit] term;

because the path attained manifests the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and non-attainment, it is not called a "fruit" when contrasted with the preceding three. Question: Why does Śūnyatā-janman cultivate *prajñāpāramitā*?
If one asks, "Is this the practice of the Great Vehicle? the answer is: it is not the cultivation of the Great Vehicle.
What is explained here is that since Śūnyatā-utpanna has realized emptiness, his emptiness is in accord with *prajñā*; he is moved by the Buddha’s empowerment to proclaim this matter.
This demonstrates how a bodhisattva cultivates the path, attains the supreme fruit, and becomes free from pride. Since the text contains four fruits, it is now divided into four sections; first:
The first fruit is divided into two parts. First is the question:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna have the thought: 'I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna'?"
The Treatise says: "I have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. This is a manifestation based on the meaning [of the teaching] to counteract the conceit of "I have attained.
If one were to think, "I have attained," that would constitute the conceit of having a self. To demonstrate the absence of such conceit, this question is asked.
△ Second, the answer.
Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? The name 'Srotāpanna' means 'one who has entered the stream,' yet there is nothing entered.
The first fruit is called the stream; it may flow either against or with [the current]. The stream of birth and death is that which the Srotāpanna person turns against."
The flow. Sentient beings follow it. Second is the flow of the Way (*mārga-srota*). Those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* follow and enter this flow;
this is what is meant here by "entering the flow. Yet, there is nothing entered, because within the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), one perceives no attainment whatsoever.
Not entering into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects—this is called a *srotāpanna*.

"Not entering" form, smell, and so forth means not following along; because one knows that form is itself empty, one goes against the flow of sensory objects, which is termed "flowing against the current.
In the first fruit (*prathama-phala*), both meanings of "reversing the flow" are fully present. △ Second, the second fruit. Furthermore:
2. First question:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a sakṛdāgāmin have such a thought as: 'I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin'?"
2. The second answer:
Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? One who is called a Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-Returner) actually has no coming or going;
it is merely designated as 'Sakṛdāgāmin.'"

After the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*), one proceeds to sever the six grades of desire-thoughts (*kāmānuśaya*). Once these have been exhausted and have moistened six future births, it is called the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*).

Furthermore, there remain three grades that together moisten one more birth; because they have not yet been severed, one must return once more to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) before they can be cut off.
Thus, one "returns once" (*sakṛdāgāmin*), yet in reality there is no coming or going. Master Zhaowang said: "One realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
The fruit. One does not perceive the marks of coming and going. △ Third, the three fruits. This also has two parts. First, the question:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have the thought: 'I have attained the fruit of Anāgāmin'?"
△ Second, the answer. Subhūti said:
"No, World-Honored One. Why is this? One who is called an Anāgāmin is so named because they do not come; yet in reality there is no coming. Therefore, they are called an Anāgāmin."
Once the nine grades of desire-thoughts have been severed, both the seeds and their manifestations are exhausted, and one will no longer be reborn in the desire realm;

thus, it is called "Non-returner" (*anāgāmin*). According to the underlying principle, one should say "there is actually no non-returning," but since the word "no" is absent from the sūtra, there is no need to add it.
△ Fourth, the four fruits. This also has two parts. First, the question.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Arhat have the thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship"? The term "Arhat" has no direct equivalent [in other languages];
it encompasses three meanings: namely, "slayer of thieves," "one who does not arise [again]," and "worthy of offerings. Furthermore, the Arhat possesses...
There are two types: those liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) and those liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

If a person of wisdom cultivates the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight recollections (*aṣṭasmṛti*), and the ten notions (as in the *Dharmadhātuanupūrvikrama*), they are called a "person who destroys [defilements]. Because the mind loathes the six desires as if they were enemies or thieves, one cultivates the nine notions as an antidote.

When performing this contemplation, although the six desires are destroyed, there is much fear. If, however, one cultivates the eight kinds of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), [fear is eliminated].

Fear is immediately eliminated. Since the desire within him has been thinned, he is furthermore free from fear. At that time, wishing to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms, he cultivates the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*).
When the tenth perception, the perception of burning (*ādahanasaṃjñā*), is accomplished, the skeleton is destroyed;
he then proceeds directly into emptiness (*ākāśa*). Thereupon, he slays all the fetters and becomes an Arhat. This person, having thus destroyed the body of desire, [attains liberation].
They do not attain the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

If, however, they are those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), they do not destroy their physical body through desire; rather, by concurrently practicing the four types of dhyāna—refined through cultivation, refinement, and perfuming—they give rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), becoming Arhats of great power who are fully endowed with the three knowledges, the eight liberations, and the attainment of cessation. As it is said regarding those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*): "By means of..."

The "emptiness" refers directly to those of simultaneous liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), who practice by combining the cultivation of both phenomena and wisdom; this is what is meant. The present text correctly concerns these individuals of simultaneous liberation.
As stated in the *Dhyānapāramitā-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-sūtra*: "An Arhat of unshakable dharma can possess the *araṇā-samādhi*.
However, if one does not clarify that there is liberation through the absence of doubt, and explains only those who possess wisdom simultaneously with concentration, why is this so?

Yes. One must know that in the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are only two types—those with wisdom-liberation (*prajñā-vimukti*) and those with both [wisdom and concentration]—because the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) they cultivate consist of only these two.
However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that it was only at the time of the compilation [of the scriptures] that "liberation through non-doubt" (*aniyata-vimukti*) appeared;

this was derived from the "liberation through both," as there were no separate meditative concentrations to be cultivated for it. Jingxi stated that the *Āgama* contains the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).

"Liberation" refers to the Arhat who is free from doubt. If one were to distinguish them as different, then based on the three types of *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness) practiced, there are variations of single, dual, or complete application. △ Second, the answer is fivefold. First, phenomena are truly nameless.
Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Truly, there is no dharma that can be called an Arhat.
From the first fruit up to the fruit of Arhatship, there is no distinct dharma; the principle is the same for all. This is the essence of the unconditioned."
There is nothing to be grasped or rejected; therefore it is said, "In truth, there is no... and so forth. △ Second, to have such thoughts constitutes attachment:
"World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to think, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' he would immediately be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span."
This demonstrates the absence of thought. If there were thought, attachment would arise. Why? Because within unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), nothing can be attained;
how then could one further form thoughts? The same applies to the preceding three fruits; the text for this is shown later.
△ Third, the description of the Buddha’s testimony and confirmation: He himself declares that he does not form such thoughts. Who, then, can be trusted? This is...
To provide testimony and inspire confidence, he recounted the Buddha’s praise:
"World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that among men I am foremost in the attainment of the Samādhi of Non-contention;
I am a foremost Arhat who is free from desire."

Regarding why Kumārajīva recounts the Buddha’s praise of Śūnyatā-utpāda (Kongsheng), Vasubandhu states: "It is for the purpose of clarifying his supreme merit and for the purpose of engendering deep faith.
As for this "supreme merit," it refers precisely to the *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-contention). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Among the disciples, Subhūti has attained the foremost *araṇā-samādhi*. One who possesses the *araṇā-samādhi* constantly observes sentient beings..."
He gives rise [to this thought] so as not to distress his mind. If one were to harbor the notion that there is something attained, it would constitute contention.

To engender deep faith, he does not speak of his own realization out of emptiness; rather, he recounts what the Buddha praised, so that those who hear it may give rise to deep faith. △ Fourth, examining oneself to sever all thoughts.
"World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought as 'I am an Arhat free from desire. World-Honored One,
if I were to harbor such a thought as 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā."
“World-Honored One, as for my not forming such a thought: [the phrase] ‘there was originally no title of World-Honored One’ should be added.

Although the Buddha praised me, I did not form such a thought. World-Honored One, had I formed such a thought, the World-Honored One would not have declared that I am a practitioner of non-contention (*araṇa-vihārin*).
*Araṇa* translates as ‘non-contention’; therefore, the Sui translation says: ‘I...’”
If one were to think, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," the World-Honored One would not have declared me foremost in the practice of non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*).
In this context, the words of a previous Buddha are cited again to make it known that [the Buddha] has severed all such thoughts.
△ Fifth, the name is true and not false.
Because Subhūti has, in reality, nothing upon which to act, he is called "Subhūti who delights in the practice of araṇā.

The *Śāstra* says: "Because there is no dharma by which one attains arhatship, and because there is nothing upon which to act, it is called 'non-contention' (araṇā) and the 'practice of non-contention.
Within this, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is established. Master Xie said: "The name he receives is not in vain; it must surely be so."
This refers to being in accordance with reality. △ Sixth, not being separated from the appearance of a Buddha. The *Śāstra* says:

Based on being free from obstacles, among the twelve types [of conditions], in order to be free from limited learning (*alpa-śruta*), one who sees a Buddha necessarily hears the Dharma; this is called "much learning" (*bahu-śruta*). The *Sūtra Commentary* states:
From here below, there is a detailed explanation of the characteristics of the practices of the Bodhisattva. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Surpassing the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas..."

[The Pratyekabuddha] enters the stage of a bodhisattva. Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, he purifies the buddha-fields. Having purified the buddha-fields, he brings sentient beings to maturity.
Having brought sentient beings to maturity, he attains all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). In the present sutra, after passing beyond the stage of an arhat, one enters the stage of a bodhisattva;
subsequently, the vow to purify the buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity is exactly the same as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin).
The characteristics described consist solely of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is truly difficult to attain.

Were it not for being far removed from distraction and contemplating the deconstruction of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, how could one reach this state? The text is divided into two parts; first, the question.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, did he obtain any dharma?

This question concerning the past is raised to interrogate Śūnyatā-janman (Subhūti) regarding the fact that, when answering the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], he saw nothing obtained. Thus, the Tathāgata here...
At that time, there was something he attained. In the Sanskrit language it is called Dīpaṃkara; here it is translated as "Light of Stability" (Dingguang) and is also named "Lamp-Lighter" (Randle).

One has not yet been able to enter *nirvāṇa*. Only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred *kalpas* does one attain *nirvāṇa*. The term "to reach" (*dài*) means that one has arrived from afar.

"This river is the place where the Buddha was born and where he traveled; because his disciples saw it with their own eyes, it is frequently cited as a metaphor. Question: Regarding the sands of the Ganges...
"How many are there? He replied, "They cannot be known by any calculation; only a Buddha and a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body can know their number. Part Two: The Answer.

II. Comparing by way of merit. This has two parts: first, showing that the merit of giving jewels is great; second, revealing that the merit of upholding this sutra is superior.

Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth: if there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures,
filled as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and gave them as a gift, would they gain much merit?
Nevertheless, this comparison further reveals the gravity of the merit. The Sūtra cites the matter of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as a provisional analogy.

One should know that the text of the eighteenth [dwelling] contains two sections; they do not concern the depth of practice and stages, but are general comparisons. The first clarifies...

This explains the causes for receiving and upholding [the teaching]. One reads because one wishes to receive it; one recites because one wishes to uphold it. The commentary states:

The two characters "reading and reciting" collectively express the text that signifies; this refers to hearing within the scriptural volumes.

The front of the text is called "reading" (dú), and the back of the text is called "reciting" (sòng). The commentary states: This refers solely to the capacity for the expressive text; because of its reception and retention, there is reading and reciting.

therefore, it is said that there is nothing taught. [Section Ten: Regarding the grasping of the ten material forms and the bodies of sentient beings, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* refutes their corresponding activities.

the first is the skillful means of subtle pulverization, which is further divided into two. First, the question:
Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many?
Since worlds are established by the accumulation of atoms, if they were now ground down again into dust, it would reveal that the world is empty and non-existent.
If the physical body were not established, one would see only atoms. To pose a hypothetical question: would these be many?
2. The Response.
Subhūti said: "Very many, World-Honored One."
△ Second, the skillful means of non-attention.
Subhūti, as for all those motes of dust, the Tathāgata has said they are not motes of dust; they are called "motes of dust" only by name.
Although the world-systems have been reduced to motes of dust, one should no longer conceive of these motes of dust as being real. This is because they are observed with the eye of wisdom.
Its true nature is fundamentally non-existent; what could possibly be apprehended? Therefore, the Tathāgata said that what is not a minute particle is called a "minute particle.

This is because, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is nothing to be conceptualized—meaning that one does not conceptualize even the skillful means (*upāya*) by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
Thus, there would be these subtle atoms, which are called the "expedient means of fine powder. To explain this briefly: first, one breaks the boundaries into atoms;

second, one breaks the atoms into empty space. If this were the case, the meaning of the Two Truths would become obscure. It is better to rely on the treatise. △ Second, refuting the image of the body of a sentient being.
The Tathāgata says that the world is not a world; it is called a "world.
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* asks: "What is meant by the 'sentient-being world'? 'World' (*loka*) refers to the flux of time, and 'realm' (*dhātu*) refers to spatial directions."
The Treatise says: "It is merely by means of the 'body of names' (nāmakāya) that one refers to sentient beings in the world;

it is simply that the skillful means of recollection is not employed, and thus the subtle and minute skillful means are no longer discussed. Thus, the mind possesses only names but lacks substantial essence;

therefore, the subtle and minute are not mentioned, because their actual nature does not exist. Since even the 'body of names' is not [ultimately] real, it is said that this is not the world. 11. Explaining Offerings.

Regarding "Making Offerings to the Tathāgata," the *Śāstra* states: Among the twelve types of abandoning obstacles, this is for the purpose of abandoning the lack of the provisions of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*).
Although one has previously contemplated the deconstruction of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the provisions of merit are not yet complete.
To complete these provisions of merit, one must make offerings to the Tathāgata. This consists of two parts; first, the question:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The thirty-two marks adorn the body of one zhang and six chi. [This concludes] section two: the answer.
"No, World-Honored One. One cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls the thirty-two marks are, in fact, no-marks; they are merely designated as the 'thirty-two marks.'"
The Commentary states: "The thirty-two marks refer to the physical body born of parents; yet these very marks are non-marks, for they are the True Suchness Dharma-body.

The reason only the physical body (janman-kāya) is indicated and not the Dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya) is that when Bodhisattvas practice Prajñāpāramitā, they are mostly born in the Desire Realm;
therefore, when approaching the Tathāgata, they speak of the physical body. If [one were to speak of] the Dharma..."
Regarding the "Dharmatā-body" (xing-shen): the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Buddha of the Dharmatā-body preaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body.

Jingxi remarked that this statement is made with reference to the realm beyond the triple world (*dharmadhātu*). I, however, say this is not so; if one considers the Lord of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, [he is the Dharmatā-body].
Regarding the claim that there is only the *janma-kāya* (birth-body), this shares the same error as the ancient masters. The *Miaoxuan* (Excellence of the Profound) quotes an ancient source stating:
"The *Prajñāpāramitā* clarifies emptiness and eliminates marks, yet it does not clarify the eternal presence of Buddha-nature; it still refers to a Buddha who is impermanent for eighty years.

Zhiyi, using the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s critique of the two bodies—the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*)—argues that the birth-body is similar to human beings, whereas the Buddha of the *dharmatā-kāya* (dharma-nature body) is the *dharmakāya*.
When a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, even the elephants that listen to the Dharma are beyond birth and death; how much more so, then, is the Buddha? Jingxi remarked:
"This is merely based on a single body to distinguish the difficulty of [the relationship between] birth and Dharma. If this were so, could it be restricted solely to the *janman-kāya* (birth-body)?
Therefore, within this context, Śūnyatā-utpanna (Śāriputra) is summoned and asked: "Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks? It is for this reason that he replies.
[Subhūti] said: "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks.
Furthermore, these thirty-two marks are but a body subject to segmentation, birth, and extinction. How can one see the Teacher of Prajñā through such a body? The Treatise says:
"When drawing near to and making offerings to the Tathāgata, one should not see the Tathāgata as the accomplishment of physical marks. Why is this?

One should see [the Buddha]. This is because one sees the Dharma-body of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). As for the perfection of marks, this refers to the thirty-two marks; yet the Dharma-body of the ultimate truth is itself non-marked.
This is truly because *prajñā* universally pervades the three teachings. A Buddha must possess both the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the Dharma-body.
If a person of the Separate or Perfect Teachings relies on the Middle Way and employs their karmic consciousness, they see the Buddha abiding in the reality-principle; thus, they behold him.
The thirty-two marks are themselves the Dharma-body, which is non-marked. Because they are identical to the Dharma, they are seen in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Their manifestation is inexhaustible; there is no need for them to arise anew. Thus, the inferior is seen as superior, and it is said: "These are called the thirty-two marks."

If one is a person of penetrating insight who contemplates phenomena based on emptiness, they perceive only the body of delimited divisions and do not see the Dharma-body that is beyond characteristics.
The present sutra speaks from the perspective of the preeminent, correctly revealing the characteristics of the supreme response-body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Dharma-nature. Question:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that the Buddha of the Dharma-nature body preaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body. Jingxi sometimes says that this refers to the [Dharmadhātu] realm.

Externally, one may make this statement; or it may be said that, regarding a single body, the two aspects of birth and dharma are distinguished. These two texts appear to differ; how then should they be distinguished?
Answer: The two texts are originally one; they should not be sought as different. Why? If one discusses them in terms of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), [they are distinct].
Thus, the marks of the *viśeṣa* (extraordinary) [Buddha] are colors belonging to the realm beyond [the triple world].

Since the lands of *paricchinna-bhāga* (segmented/limited existence) originally lack these marks, if the karmic conditions of those in the realm beyond arise, the Buddha likewise responds to them. Therefore, it is said that this teaching is formulated in reference to the realm beyond.

If explained in terms of essence, there is only one Buddha; yet for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests both superiority and inferiority. That is to say, it is based solely on this one [Buddha].
The body manifests the dharma of differentiated birth. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
When the Buddha wished to preach the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he sat upon the lion throne and manifested his most supreme body, with its radiant form and majestic, towering majesty.
By means of this spiritual power, he moved the sentient beings; those who had faith all attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Among them, for those who harbored doubts, the Buddha revealed—
They attained faith and understanding regarding the eternal body (*nitya-kāya*), each saying to themselves: "That which we now behold is the Buddha’s true body.
This applied even to the time of the Buddha’s initial birth, his first attainment of enlightenment, and his first turning of the wheel of Dharma;

they all regarded it as this very body, thinking, "This is the Buddha’s true body. By this one may know that [the perception] has shifted from the sixteen-foot body that is constantly seen toward the *parinirvāṇa*.

If, at the first assembly, he manifests a state of veneration appropriate for the assembly of the dharma-nature beyond the realms, those who are unsuited to behold it shall again find that veneration concealed;
instead, he manifests his birth-body (*janma-kāya*). By means of this birth-body, he fully participates in all the assemblies of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

If this is so, then it is merely a single body manifesting as superior or inferior. By this principle, one should know that the two texts follow the same track; there is no need for further inquiry. Question:

Regarding the manifestation of these displays, how do their similarities and differences compare? Answer: The "Distinguished" (zunte) [body] is one and the same, yet the marks and signs (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) differ.
Because the marks differ, there are cases where manifestation is required and cases where it is not; there are cases with spatial limits and cases without limits.

They are different. Because they are the same. They are both the marks of the lotus pedestal. Therefore, the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) clarifies that the *zunte* (special body of the Buddha) appears alone, while the *ji* (Records/Commentary) points to their identity.
Regarding Maudgalyāyana not fathoming the sound [of the Buddha], the *Zhiguan* (Stopping and Contemplation) clarifies that Maudgalyāyana did not fathom its sound.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "The body that sits upon the lotus pedestal to receive its office is also of this same aspect.

Thus we know that when Jingxi refers to these two locations as mutually indicating one another, it is to demonstrate that the *zunte* (exalted special body) is identical to the manifested form of the lotus pedestal.

△ 12. Because of generating diligence by remaining far removed from gain and offerings. The Treatise says: Among the twelve [factors] for departing from obstacles, it is for the sake of abandoning the savoring of gain, offerings, and so forth that arise from indolence.
Although one has previously contemplated the destruction of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), because one possesses the provisions of merit, one still makes offerings to the Tathāgata;
yet, fearing that one might again become indolent in body and mind due to a craving for gain and offerings—△
One must distance oneself from such states and arouse a mind of diligence to uphold and expound this sutra.

Just as Sadāprarudita, desiring to hear the Prajñāpāramitā, wept sorrowfully in a secluded grove for seven days and seven nights; and for seven years he practiced walking and standing, neither sitting nor lying down, constantly thinking, "When shall I hear the Prajñāpāramitā?
having no other thought whatsoever. This is what it means to arouse diligence, as opposed to indolence.
It is thus destroyed. This consists of two parts: first, the calculation of the benefits; second, praising the person for their reverence of the Dharma. The first part also has two sections:
first, presenting the characteristics of the merit of material offerings.

Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who were to give away their lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in acts of charity, this relinquishing of life and body, when compared, would be far more weighty than the previous gift of the seven treasures filling the great trichiliocosm. As it says in the Treatise:
If one were to give away as many bodies and lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, therein the body would experience exhaustion and the mind would suffer from feverish affliction;
because of these two factors, one might either regress from or fail to initiate that diligence. What does this demonstrate?
Even by relinquishing such a multitude of bodies, one’s own resulting merit would not equal the merit of this [present practice]. Why is this so? Because of attachment to a single body.
"Indolence, etc. The commentary states: "Those who have already applied diligence may regress; those who have not yet applied diligence do not initiate it.
Therefore, it says 'if one regresses,' etc. It further states: "There are those who sacrifice their bodies but do not sacrifice their lives, such as Śibi when he substituted himself for the pigeon;

there are those who sacrifice their bodies and immediately sacrifice their lives, such as the *sattva* when he fed the tiger. This is precisely what is meant by sacrificing both body and life. △ Second.
To manifest the excellence of the benefits of the Dharma:
if there should be another person who, from this sutra, even receives and upholds as little as a four-line verse and explains it to others.
The merit thereof is exceedingly great.

Master Xie said: "To give away one's body and life through material charity does not exempt one from further birth; to widely uphold even four lines of verse extinguishes accumulated karma and brings the Way to fruition.
△ Second, praising the person for their reverence for the Dharma, which has two parts. First, revering the Dharma.
At that time, Subhūti, upon hearing this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent.
The commentary states: "The phrase 'deeply understanding' does not exceed two meanings: first, understanding the meaning of the Mahāyāna as emptiness;

second, understanding the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s benefit for others. Understanding [the meaning of] emptiness is like saying they have entered together into the *dharmatā*; understanding [the meaning of] benefiting others..."
It is also said that they were not yet involved in this matter; however, this is not so. Furthermore, regarding the understanding of the Mahāyāna as emptiness—is it implicit or explicit?
If it is implicit, then since it was already understood through the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras), how could it only be understood upon reaching the Prajñā[pāramitā]?

If it is explicit, then one should have turned from the Small [Vehicle] into the Great [Vehicle], thereby being involved in this matter; why then say they "entered the dharma-nature together"? Now, it is said that emptiness arises...
Having arrived at this assembly, they are no longer as bewildered and despondent as when they previously cast aside their alms bowls;

their minds are now clear and composed, and through the empowerment of the Buddha’s power, they hear this Mahāyāna and deeply understand its meaning and intent. If this is so, one might ask: did those of the two vehicles not also possess knowledge of the Great [Vehicle] in the past?
It must be understood that although they knew there was a "Great" [Vehicle], they did not know of the distinct, wondrous principle realized by the Bodhisattvas. This is because...

Because they do not know the distinct principle, they remain as ignorant regarding the Great [Vehicle] as they were before; yet, from their own perspective, they claim to have a profound understanding.
Question: If those born of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) do not know the distinct principle, then they have nothing realized within themselves, and what they speak lacks any expressive power. Answer:
Since they are empowered by the Buddha’s power, it is identical to the Buddha’s own teaching.
With tears streaming down his face and weeping piteously, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One! That the Buddha should preach such a profound sutra as this;
from my past until now, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard a sutra such as this."
As for those who weep and wail with grief: moved outwardly by their profound reverence for the Dharma, they shed tears like falling rain;
this is the ultimate expression of such devotion. Since my time at the Deer Park until now, I have never before heard such a Dharma-gate as this.
The supreme merit it brings is far greater than that of sacrificing countless bodies and lives in almsgiving.
Having given this gift, no further superior merit was mentioned. Did he not then arouse diligence? Thus, although Śūnyatājanman heard the Mahāyāna, he did not grasp it;
although he had already realized it while riding [the vehicle], he did not doubt it. It was only upon arriving at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* that he finally recognized his former fault.
△ Second, praising the person. This is divided into two parts: first, the actual praise; second, the corroboration. The first part is further divided into two. First, a general overview...
Praise through Faith. Second, specific praise concerning future lives. This section also has two parts. First, faith and understanding upon hearing the sutra:
"World-Honored One, if there should be someone who hears this sutra and their mind of faith becomes pure, they will immediately give rise to the mark of reality. You should know that..."
This person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
The *Śāstra* says: "If, within this Dharma, one gives rise to the notion that it is as it truly is [the meaning], this is to avoid such faults.
The *Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, if there are those who hear this sūtra and their faith becomes pure," because Prajñā is untainted, they immediately give rise to [it].

Regarding the "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): because the *dharmakāya* has emerged from its entanglements, one should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit, and so forth.
Within this very true reality, it is for the purpose of abandoning conceptualization regarding true reality. △ Second, faith and understanding of the signless (*animitta*).
“World-Honored One, this true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is itself the absence of marks (*alakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name ‘true mark.
This true mark is, in reality, without marks; thus it is the absence of marks. Because it pervades all marks, it is called the ‘true mark. II.
Praising [the Dharma] with reference to future generations. This has two parts. First, manifesting the present through a subsequent observation.
“World-Honored One, for me now to hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it would not be difficult.

Śūnyatā-jāta, reflecting upon yourself and having been commanded to turn the wheel of teaching and take charge of the property, to hear this profound sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it would not be difficult.
To ‘believe, understand, accept, and uphold’ means: one believes because of receiving the text, and one upholds because of maintaining its meaning.”
[The Buddha] said:

"If, in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there are sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, such persons shall be the most rare and extraordinary.
Why is this? Because these people are free from the mark of self, the mark of person, and the mark of sentient being."
The mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span—these are all non-marks. Why is this so? Because the mark of a self is itself a non-mark;
the marks of a person, a sentient being, and a life-span are likewise non-marks.

The treatise states: In order to inspire shame and remorse in those bodhisattvas who are attached to gain and offerings and are indolent, [it is shown that] even at a future time when the True Dharma is extinguished, there will still be bodhisattvas who uphold this dharma-gate, free from the grasping of self and person as well as the grasping of dharmas.
How is it that you, during the flourishing of the True Dharma, remain far removed from its practice?
This gives rise to shame and remorse; this is merely an exhortation expressed by referring to the present through the lens of the future. The *Śāstra* states:

"This person lacks the marks of a self," which demonstrates the non-appropriation of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*, i.e., emptiness of persons). "The marks of a self are themselves the marks of non-self," which demonstrates the non-appropriation of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*, i.e., emptiness of phenomena).
△ Second, emulating the training of all Buddhas.
Why is this? Because being free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is precisely what is called "all Buddhas.
The *Śāstra* states: "This reveals the characteristics of the bodhisattvas' compliant training. Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have already transcended all marks..."
Therefore, we too should train in this manner. These scriptural passages are taught for the purpose of abandoning the regression of diligence.

△ Second, the section on "Accomplishing through Description" has two parts. First, generating faith upon hearing the sutra. The treatise states: "This is for the purpose of abandoning those who do not initiate diligence."

The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is truly rare."

"Thus it is, thus it is" is a statement of confirmation. "Not startled, not terrified, and not afraid": the treatise states that because of such startlement and so forth, one does not initiate diligence.
Within the Śrāvaka vehicle, the World-Honored One taught the existence of phenomena (*dharma*) and the existence of emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
when hearing this sūtra, one is startled upon hearing that phenomena do not exist, and terrified upon hearing that emptiness does not exist.
When they contemplate this, because they cannot reconcile it with their own principle that "two things do not exist together," they are afraid.

Thus we know that what is taught as "existent dharmas" in the Śrāvaka vehicle refers to truly existent dharmas, and what is taught as "emptiness" refers to a partial or one-sided emptiness. This is because in the Lesser Vehicle, existence and emptiness are not identical;

however, now hearing that in the Prajñāpāramitā, existence and emptiness are mutually identical—that phenomena are themselves emptiness—they are startled upon hearing that phenomena are emptiness, and startled upon hearing emptiness.

It is because they are merely provisional that there is fear; it is because they cannot correspond with the principle of non-existence within those two [extremes] when one reflects upon them that there is dread.
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, does not arouse diligence, they are identical to the śrāvakas in giving rise to alarm and fear.
Thus, if the mind is not alarmed or afraid, one will necessarily arouse great diligence. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says:

If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is neither startled nor terrified, one should know that this bodhisattva will before long receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of awakening;
it will not exceed the time of one or two Buddhas. The Commentary states: "Hearing the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) does not cause alarm;

hearing the contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*) does not cause fear; hearing the skillful means (*upāya*) does not cause dread. II. The Superiority of What is Taught. The Treatise says: "This Dharma is like..."
This is supreme. You all should not be negligent. Why is this?
Subhūti, what the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not, in fact, a foremost pāramitā;
it is designated as the foremost pāramitā.

Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata says they are equal," the treatise states that this demonstrates that those immeasurable Buddhas likewise teach that the *prajñāpāramitā* is superior to the other *pāramitās*, and is therefore called "the foremost.
The Sūtra says "not" because it realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), which is quiescent, transcendent, and free from conceptual elimination;
yet it further says "is" because, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), there is indeed something [to be attained].

Because it is so stated. △ Thirteen: The Characteristics of Forbearance (*kṣānti*). The Treatise says: Among the twelve types [of practices] based on being free from obstacles, this is for the sake of abandoning the inability to endure suffering.
This consists of two parts: first, the ability to endure; second, the abandonment of the inability to endure. The first [ability to endure] further has three parts.
The first is that which is capable of enduring.
Subhūti, the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) is, as the Tathāgata has taught, not a perfection of patience.
In the Sanskrit language it is called kṣānti, which is translated here as "patience" (rěn'ǔ). The Commentary states: "The inner mind is able to endure external objects that cause humiliation.

The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra says: "There are two kinds of patience: first, patience toward sentient beings (sattva-kṣānti); second, patience regarding phenomena (dharma-kṣānti). There are two types of patience toward sentient beings. First—

Regarding respectful offerings and veneration, one is able to endure them without becoming conceited. Second, regarding verbal abuse, physical assault, and injury, one is able to endure them without harboring anger or resentment.

There are two types of patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*): first, those that are not mental factors (*acaitasika*), such as cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, sickness, death, and so forth;
second, those that are mental factors (*caitasika*), such as anger, malice, sorrow, and even all manner of wrong views. Now...
Regarding "patience" (*kṣānti*): within the two types of patience—regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and regarding birth (*janman*)—it refers to the second meaning in both cases.

The Treatise states: "What is that which is able to endure? It is the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). If one realizes the selflessness of phenomena, what honor or disgrace could one not endure?

Those who study the Buddha's teachings should engrave this upon their hearts and record it upon their girdles. 2. The Characteristics of Patience. The Treatise asks: "How should the characteristics of patience be understood? If...
When he encounters the arising of evil within himself and others, because he is devoid of the notion of a self, no thought of anger arises;
nor does he conceive the notion of existence regarding the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), nor the notion of non-existence regarding that which is not a perfection.

Why is this? Subhūti, when in the past I was King Kali and my body was cut to pieces, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span.
In Sanskrit, this is *Kali*; here it is translated as "Evil-Born" (*Akṣema-janman*) and is also called "Utterly Wicked. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
When the Seer Kṣāntivādin was practicing patience and cultivating loving-kindness in a great forest, King Kali, accompanied by his court ladies, entered the forest for recreation.
After eating, he rested briefly, while the ladies gathered flowers among the trees; they saw this seer and paid him increased reverence.
She prostrated herself and remained there for a long time without departing. When the king awoke and did not see his maidservant, he drew his sword and followed her tracks.
Seeing her standing before the rishi, his arrogance and jealousy flared up; with eyes blazing with rage, he brandished his sword and asked the rishi, "What are you doing?"
The seer replied, “I am here now, practicing patience and cultivating loving-kindness. The king said, “How do you practice patience? I shall test you now.
He then used a sharp sword to cut off his ears and nose and sever his hands and feet, asking him, “Does your mind waver?
He replied, “I practice loving-kindness and patience; my mind does not waver. The king said, “Who would believe you? At that time, the seer—
The man then made a vow: "If I have truly practiced loving-kindness and patience, let my blood turn to milk.
Immediately, his blood transformed into milk. The king was greatly surprised and departed. At that time, a forest spirit, for the sake of the rishi, sent lightning and thunderbolts;
the king was killed and died without returning to his palace. (Kāli was none other than Cunda. The *Śāstra* says: "As it was with me in the past..."
When King Kali cut and mangled my body, at that time I had no notion of a self, nor did I have the notion of non-existence, nor even the notion of neither existence nor non-existence.
Therefore, it should be known that this was to demonstrate abiding in the true nature (*dharmatā*); thus, I felt neither sorrow nor vexation. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: Question:
A bodhisattva’s body is not made of wood or stone; how is it that they feel no resentment when their body is cut and mangled? Answer:
Some say that because the Bodhisattva has long cultivated *kṣānti* (patience), he does not experience sorrow or vexation.
Others say it is because the Bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, has deeply cultivated great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and is thus beyond the ordinary mind.

Others say it is because the Bodhisattva has cultivated *prajñā* and transformed his body, acting as the fruition of the retribution of *prajñā*. Others say that the Bodhisattva’s body is not one of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), but is that which has emerged from the three [realms].
The body of the dharma-nature of the realms (*dhātu-dharmatā-kāya*) abides in the untainted (*anāsrava*); thus, the body is like wood or stone. The Commentary states:

"Now, examining the treatise, the first three meanings refer to the body born of parents, while the last one reveals the body of dharma-nature. One should know that these two bodies cannot be taken up exclusively.
If it were only the body born of parents, which has not yet severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*), how could it be cut or dismembered without [the perception of] self?"

Regarding the "equal marks" (*samasamalakṣaṇa*): if one speaks of the *dharmatākāya*, which does not depend upon the segmented [birth], how can there be the matter of having one's limbs severed joint by joint or of blood and milk?

Truly, it is because the Bodhisattva has long cultivated loving-kindness and patience (*maitrī-kṣānti*), as well as practiced *prajñāpāramitā*, thereby destroying the two attachments to self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*) and attaining the *dharmatākāya*. Yet, he re-enters the segmented [birth] to manifest the practice of patience. As it is said:
Because of great compassion, he does not abide in nirvāṇa; rather, he focuses specifically on the realm of phenomena to cultivate the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā). Question:
Some rely on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states that when the Buddha was a bodhisattva, his three poisons were not yet exhausted, and he acted as a rishi named Kṣānti.
Even when his ears, nose, hands, and feet were severed by a wicked king, he gave rise to no evil thoughts nor uttered any evil words.

At that time, such was his state even before attaining the Way; how much more so after attaining Bodhi? Since it is said that he had not yet exhausted the three poisons, this proves he possessed a body born of parents;
how then can it be called a Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*)? Answer: This statement is incorrect. Why? One must understand this.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) cites Kātyāyanīputra to show that the meaning of the Tripiṭaka is not the Prajñā [Pāramitā], thereby clarifying the status of the Mahābodhisattva.

The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) states: "The *Śāstra* cites Kātyāyanīputra to clarify the meaning of the Bodhisattva; one should know that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites him for the purpose of refutation.
If this is so, how can it be said that the treatise relies on [Kātyāyanīputra] to demonstrate the object of refutation in order to extend the Prajñā?
"O Great Bodhisattva. △ Third, the types of patience are divided into two. First, patience toward extreme suffering.

Why is this? When my limbs and joints were severed piecemeal in the past, if there had been any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.
