Master Zhao said: "Because there is no anger or resentment, there is no mark of self or person. △ Second, the patience of continuity:
"Subhūti, furthermore, he recalls that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, he was a rishi of forbearance; throughout those lifetimes..."
There is no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
Even when his body was cut and mangled—an injury of extreme suffering—this continued in uninterrupted succession for five hundred lifetimes.
Guṇaprabha says: "This reveals that in the past, before encountering the evil king, he had already severed the notions of 'self' and so forth throughout many births."
Having already severed the notion of a self, when testing the rishi, it was evident that he was not one still bound by the physical body. II.
Second, being free from the inability to endure: "As I formerly suffered when King Kali cut and mangled my limbs, even such extreme suffering I was able to endure;
how much more so that which is external to the body—how could I not endure it? For this reason, a bodhisattva who wishes to give rise to bodhicitta...
Focus the mind. One must endure all forms of suffering; herein there are two aspects. First is the general characteristic.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should depart from all marks and resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The treatise states: "Because of the three kinds of suffering, one does not wish to resolve upon the mind [of enlightenment];
therefore, it is said that one should abandon all marks (*sarvanimitta*). Herein, 'all marks' is used to reveal the characteristics of these three kinds of suffering.
If a bodhisattva cannot endure them, they will be moved by the three sufferings; hence, it says 'one should abandon them,' etc. △ Second, the specific characteristics: namely, the three.

The various aspects of suffering: first, the suffering of cyclic existence; second, the suffering of conflict among sentient beings; third, the suffering of lacking resources for enjoyment. Regarding the first section:
one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
The treatise states: "If one is attached to form and so forth, one will become exhausted within the suffering of saṃsāra;
therefore, the bodhicitta will not arise. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "A bodhisattva practicing prajñā should not abide in the ten powers or the fearlessnesses.
If the Buddha were without fault regarding the dharmas, then one should abide [in them]. If the bodhisattva lacks the Buddha-dharmas, what would there be to discuss?"
Regarding the term "abiding," the Commentator explains: When a bodhisattva cultivates merit, they often give rise to heavy attachment; therefore, it is said that this should not be done.

One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. If the mind has an abiding, then it is not truly abiding. For this reason, the Buddha said that a bodhisattva’s mind should not abide in form when practicing giving.
A mind that abides nowhere is the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). If the mind has an abode, it is not truly abiding. Vasubandhu said:
"If the mind abides in dharmas such as form (*rūpa*), that mind does not abide in bodhi. Therefore, the Buddha taught that the mind of a bodhisattva always practices equanimity (*upekṣā*);
how could there be any abiding? Thus it is said: "One should not abide in form while practicing giving. This...
This should be explained by way of three kinds of giving. △ Second, the suffering of sentient beings' mutual opposition.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner.
The Tathāgata says that all marks are indeed non-marks; furthermore, he says that all sentient beings are indeed not sentient beings.
The treatise says: "One practices equanimity for the sake of all sentient beings; how then could one give rise to anger toward them?
Because one is unable to be without sentient beings and the perception of sentient beings, due to these causes and conditions, one becomes weary when encountering opposition from sentient beings.
Therefore, the Tathāgata reveals both the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, teaching that all [beings are empty]."
The characteristic of sentient beings is a provisional designation without reality; therefore, it is a non-characteristic. This is because there is no self in persons.

Furthermore, since it is taught that the aggregates (*skandha*) and dharmas of all sentient beings are fundamentally empty, they are not sentient beings. This is because there is no self in phenomena (*dharma*).

If one realizes that persons and phenomena are fundamentally empty and forgets the attachment to persons and phenomena, then one will be able to practice patience and will not conflict with sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata speaks what is true, speaks what is real, speaks according to reality, speaks without deception,
and speaks without deviation.

The Treatise states: "One desires to have faith in the Tathāgata and is thus able to endure. Within this context, 'speaking the true' is for the purpose of revealing the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
'speaking the real' is for the purpose of revealing the characteristics of affliction and purification within the practice of conventional truth."

Regarding "truth" therein: it is because this practice is afflicted and this practice is purified. Regarding "as-it-is": it is because it is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding "not otherwise": it is because within the cultivation of the ultimate truth, there exist the characteristics of affliction and purification.
However, among the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) in the treatise, the first two propositions correspond to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the latter two...

Regarding these phrases: in contrast to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), both are the first phrase that demonstrates the characteristics of the truths. The subsequent phrase serves for practice.
If this is so, then each of the two truths possesses its own characteristics regarding the purification of afflictions through practice. To distinguish them, the Commentary states:

To say that the practice of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) consists of transforming others by emerging into the provisional, characterized by the purification of *āsrava* (defilements) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*);
and that the practice of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) consists of personally contemplating principle, characterized by the purification of the afflictions of views, thought, and ignorance,
as well as the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)— this explanation is not correct.
Now it is said: within the two truths, both contain the three delusions and the three wisdoms. In the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the meanings are differentiated;
by relying upon this for cultivation, delusion and wisdom remain far apart. Thus it is said, "this practice is affliction, this practice is purity"—this is what is called true speech.

In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), although delusion and wisdom are momentarily distinguished, the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such that delusion and wisdom are non-dual. Regarding this...
This refers to speech that is not otherwise. This sutra encompasses both the Perfect (Yuan) and the Distinct (Bie) teachings;

since the practices cultivated by the two types of capacities differ, it is explained here in terms of the characteristics of the Two Truths. Question: Regarding these five phrases of this sutra, I do not yet understand to which category the phrase "non-deceptive speech" belongs.
Answer: It is absent in the Sui translation, but present in the Qin version. As the commentary states: "One should know that the four phrases are based on..."
The Dharma is spoken; it is not deceptive; it is taught to others. Four [aspects] are specific and one is general; that was brief while this is detailed.
Subhūti, as for the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata, this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.
The treatise states: Having explained these true words and so forth, there may arise within them an attachment to the nature of verbal expression.
To dispel this, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti, the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor unreal. As for "neither real":
As it is said: because their nature does not exist as expressed by words, the nature of language is empty. Regarding "there is no falsehood":
because they possess intrinsic nature that does not conform to verbal expression, although they are empty, there is that which is spoken. △ Third, the suffering of lacking resources for enjoyment.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells with the mind fixed on phenomena while practicing generosity, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing at all.
If a bodhisattva practices generosity with a mind that does not dwell on phenomena, it is like a person with eyes who,
when the light of the sun shines upon them, sees various forms.
Those who, lacking the wisdom of discernment, become attached to material things while practicing giving and seek after its karmic rewards, are shrouded by craving and do not understand renunciation;
they are like those who have entered darkness and do not know where they are going.
If, however, one practices giving without attachment to material things, it is like a person with eyes who, when the night has passed and the sun rises, sees all manner of forms. Following this...
Regarding "the direction of the mind," the treatise states: When that night of ignorance has passed and the sun of wisdom has arisen, one perceives it as it truly is.
It must be understood that this "ignorance" is merely the ignorance of the secondary branches—the afflictions of views and thought. Why?

Because giving performed while abiding in marks already results in the three realms, which is like the darkness of night; now, to extinguish this darkness—is this not precisely the eradication of views and thoughts? △ Fourteen: Departure.

Regarding the "taste of tranquility," the *Śāstra* states: Among the twelve [factors] based on the removal of obstacles, in order to avoid the deficiency of the accumulations for wisdom (*jñāna-sambhāra*), one desires to possess these accumulations and thus engages in upholding, reading, reciting, and so forth of this dharma-gate. The *Śāstra* further states:
Within this, in order to eliminate the distractions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), five kinds of supreme merits are revealed as being in correspondence with the Dharma.
First, the Tathāgata’s mindfulness and approach; second, the gathering of merit; third, the praise of the Dharma and its practice;
fourth, the offerings of the devas; and fifth, the extinction of offenses. Based on this, the text is divided into five sections. First is the Tathāgata’s mindfulness and approach.
Subhūti, in future ages, if there are good men or good women who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra,
the Tathāgata, by means of the Buddha’s wisdom, will fully know these people and fully see these people.

Thus, in this section, it mentions only "upholding, receiving, reading, and reciting," but does not mention "explaining it to others. However, in the four subsequent passages, all include "explaining it to others.
One must understand that since these [first] sections involve the Tathāgata’s mindfulness and personal attendance, they pertain primarily to one's own practice (*sva-caryā*).
As for the four subsequent passages, they include both oneself and the transformation of others (*parārtha*). Therefore, the verse says: "This is for the sake of maturing oneself; the rest..."

Regarding "transforming sentient beings" and "knowing fully those who are equal [to them]": this reveals the Tathāgata’s mindful recollection and close attendance toward those who receive, uphold, and maintain this sutra.
The treatise states: "The Tathāgata knows them with Buddha-wisdom; the Tathāgata sees them with the Buddha-eye.
II. Gathering Merit. This also has two parts. First, the general gathering.
All shall attain the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless merit.
By virtue of receiving and upholding this sutra, they accomplish such blessings and virtues. △ Second, the comparison, which has two parts.
First, the number of times the body is sacrificed.
Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were, during the first part of the day, to give away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;
and during the middle part of the day, again give away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;

and during the latter part of the day, likewise give away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—continuing in this manner for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, giving away their bodies.
However, in the preceding passage, one merely relinquished the body and life of a single Ganges River [of beings]; here, one gives three Ganges Rivers daily for many kalpas.
This is superior to the former. In the former case, both body and life were relinquished; here, one relinquishes only the body but does not relinquish life.
Thus, the former is superior to this. If that is so, it is merely a general comparison of differences in the amount of precious things given to discuss gradual transformation.

Even if one were to give away three bodies as many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges every day—an act of great renunciation and sacrifice—it would still be the functioning of a mind that grasps at something;
it does not equal the merit of upholding and reciting this sutra with a mind of non-attainment. Therefore, [the latter] is superior to the former.
This was proposed as a hypothetical example in order to compare the superiority of their merits; in reality, such a thing does not exist. Master Zhaolun said:

"From dawn until the hour of the Dragon (7–9 AM) is called the first portion of the day; from the hour of the Dragon until the hour of the Sheep (9 AM–3 PM) is called the middle portion of the day; from the hour of the Sheep until the hour of the Dog (3–7 PM)..."
This is called the "latter portion of the day. △ Second, the comparison of the superiority of merit:
If there were another person who, upon hearing this sutra, believed with faith and did not oppose it, their merit would surpass that [of the former]; how much more so if they were to copy it!

"Regarding 'receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it for others—how much more so for writing it down,' etc.: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, in the 'Chapter on the Gift of Dharma' (*Dharmadāna-parivarta*), states:

'To transform sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and cause them to attain the six supernatural powers is not equal to writing down the *Prajñāpāramitā* and causing others to read and recite it; furthermore, by means of this, one causes others to read [it].'"
The merit of reciting [this scripture] is not equal to that of right mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, the merit of this mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā* is not equal to that of expounding it for others so that they may easily understand it.
Thus, by comparing them in sequence, it is shown that explaining it for others is superior. △ Third, praising the Dharma and its practice, which is threefold. First, praising the Dharma.
Subhūti, to speak in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
The Tathāgata has taught it for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle; he has taught it for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
The treatise states: "Inconceivable" means it is realized only by oneself. "Incomparable" means there is nothing equal to or superior to it.
Furthermore, as for "realized by oneself": when one realizes that the merit of this sutra is inconceivable, one then extols this sutra oneself.
As for "there being nothing equal or superior": when one weighs the merit of this sutra, there is nothing equal to it.

"Those who surpass this sutra"—this is a praise directed specifically at others [of the partial] Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna). "Spoken for the sake of those who aspire to the Mahāyāna"—this excludes the Small Vehicle;
thus we know that if one is not a suitable vessel for the Dharma, it is not bestowed. Among the three vehicles, it is not spoken for the sake of those who give rise to the mind of the two vehicles;
it is spoken for the sake of those who give rise to the mind of the Supreme Vehicle—this excludes the partial. According to the *Śāstra*, this constitutes accomplishment.

It is of an incomparable meaning. Within this, it is "supreme" because other vehicles cannot reach it; it is "most excellent" because the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations are purified.
Herein, the term "bodhisattva" is shown to apply generally across both the partial (Hīnayāna) and the universal (Mahāyāna);

thus, it is said that "other vehicles cannot reach it," while only the Perfect [Vehicle] is called supreme. Because it can purify the two obscurations, it is said to "accomplish the incomparable meaning."
...and so forth. △ Second, praising the person. The Treatise says: "Praising the practice; the practice is itself the person. This is divided into two parts. First, the general statement:
"If there is anyone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it to others, the Tathāgata fully knows this person; he fully sees [them]."
These people all achieve fulfillment.
What kind of merit does this realization and vision fulfill? △ Second, the explanation:
"immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit. Such people as these...

To shoulder the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Tathāgata—that is, the merit of this sutra—is such that it cannot be measured by the mind, nor can it be fully expressed by speech; it has no limit that can be reached.
Therefore, it is called "inconceivable merit. As for "shouldering," the *Śāstra* states: "to carry *bodhi* upon one's shoulders."

Because it is a heavy burden. This [explanation] fully utilizes the meaning of the entire sutra by means of both the subject and the object. The Sutra praises the person who propagates [the teaching], saying "shoulder-bearing" (hé-dàn, level tone);
the Treatise, with respect to the Dharma being propagated, says "heavy burden" (zhòng-dàn, departing tone). △ Third, distinguishing what is not [the true teaching].
Why is this? Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span;
they will therefore be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others.
Since this sutra is taught for those who aspire to the Mahāyāna, those who delight in the lesser Dharma cannot hear or receive it.
Those who delight in the lesser are the followers of the two vehicles; those who cling to views such as self and person are ordinary worldlings.
As the Sui translation states: "If one delights in the lesser Dharma, one will be unable to accept, uphold, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others."

[The Buddha] said: "It is impossible that one who holds the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a person, or the view of a life-span could receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, and explain this Dharma-gate for others. The commentary explains:

when the sutra says "those who delight in inferior dharmas," it refers to those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles. When the sutra says "if there be those who hold [the view of] a self," etc., [it means the same].
"Seeing... even to... upholding [the Dharma]—there is no such possibility," means that there are those who hold the view of a self and sentient beings, yet claim for themselves to be bodhisattvas.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "One must use wisdom to contemplate and know the true mark of all dharmas.

Thus we know that ordinary people are like those blind from birth, while those of the two vehicles are like those with impaired vision; they do not understand what they hear because they lack the eye of wisdom.

Because they lack the eye of wisdom, even upon hearing [the teaching], they do not discern it. Thus we know that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are both incapable of hearing the *prajñā*.
This is a summary concluding the preceding points regarding how ordinary beings and followers of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) are unable to listen to and receive [the teaching].
If one reads this passage, it must be cross-referenced with the Sui dynasty translation. △ The Offerings of the Four Heavens.
Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be found, it should be venerated by all the worlds—devas, humans, and asuras.
You should know that such a place is itself a stupa; one should pay homage, prostrate, and circumambulate it with reverence.
One scatters various flowers and incense upon that spot.
Master Xie said: "Since this ground is a locus of insentient dharmas, its value lies in the humans and devas; it is not held in high esteem [in itself].
△ Fifth, the extinction of karmic offenses, which has two parts. First, the actual extinction of offenses.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, yet is treated with contempt by others, it is because of their karmic offenses from previous lives which would have caused them to fall into the evil realms;
however, by virtue of being treated with contempt by people in the present life, [those offenses are exhausted].
"Karmic offenses from previous lives will be immediately extinguished, and one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding the passage 'if one upholds this sutra, one will be treated with contempt by others,' such instances of humiliation have immeasurable forms;
it is to demonstrate these that the term 'contempt' is used. The sutra’s statement that "one shall attain *anuttara-bodhi*" reveals...

This is shown because it extinguishes transgressions. It is not merely that transgressions are extinguished; by the power of the sutra, one shall also attain Bodhi. Regarding "transgressions and karma from previous lives":
since karma extends across the three periods of time, one must know that these are fixed karmas (*niyata-karma*). Fixed karma cannot be expiated through ordinary means;
however, by practicing Prajñā, one merely transforms the heavy into the light. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The Bodhisattva practices..."
"By means of Prajñā, all grave offenses are experienced in the present life. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains:

"Grave offenses from previous lives that ought to result in rebirth in hell, because one practices Prajñā, are experienced in the present life. It is, for example, like a heavy prisoner who is destined for death [but is released]."
Those who possess power will protect them, so that they shall suffer only the lash and the staff. △ Second, comparing victory and defeat.
This consists of three parts. First, citing the merit of deeds:
"Subhūti, I recall that in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I encountered him."
He made offerings to and served eight hundred and forty trillion nayutas of Buddhas, none of whom he passed by in vain.
The *Śāstra* states: "As I recall the past," and so forth; this demonstrates his majestic power (*anubhāva*), which is the majesty of the mass of merit (*puṇyaskandha*).
Power. Because the mass of merit possessed by that [person] is far superior and exalted, one should know that "exceeding incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) means exceeding even the former.
"Not in vain" means never being separated from making offerings. *Asaṃkhyeya* is translated here as "innumerable.
*Kalpa*, in its full form, is translated as "discriminating time. *Nayuta* refers to ten billion.
Ten lakṣas make one koṭi; ten koṭis make one nayuta. △ Second, revealing the power of the sutra:
If there should be another person who, in the final age at the end of time, is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain—compared to [the former]...
The merit from my offerings to all the Buddhas does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth, nor ten million billionth part;
indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.
Making offerings is a merit derived from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Upholding the sutra is the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*) of Prajñā. Master Sengzhao said:
"This clarifies that the merit obtained from making offerings to all Buddhas is not equal to the merit of upholding the sutra;
therefore, one can swiftly realize Bodhi. △ Third, exhorting faith, which has two parts. First, fully explaining the prevention of doubt.
Subhūti, if good men or good women, in the final age at the end of time, were to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra,
the merit they would thereby obtain— if I were to describe it in its entirety— some who hear it might have their minds become deranged or fall into doubt and lack faith.
However, although the above has compared and demonstrated the abundance of merit, it is still but a brief explanation.

Were it to be explained in further detail, listeners would become suspicious and their minds would surely fall into confusion. As the treatise states: "Because this is shown to be so vast, some might regard it as a cause for madness."
Or one may obtain the fruit of a distracted mind. Regarding "one who is full of doubt": the fox is a beast; it is also called a jackal (*śṛgāla*).

Its nature is characterized by much suspicion, hence it is used as a metaphor. Alas! If the mind believes the Dharma, the Dharma immediately colors the mind. To be hesitant and full of doubt is like an overturned vessel [that cannot hold water]. The Commentary states:
"In the Mahāyāna, both the sin of slandering the faith and the merit of believing it are grave. This sutra, for the time being, speaks only of the merit obtained through belief."
[This concludes the section on] Merit. Various sutras fully explain the transgressions incurred by slandering [this teaching]. II. Concluding Summary to Reveal the Dharma Gate:
Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable.
The treatise states: One should know that as for this "other power" (*paraprabhāva*) and "that much" (*tadbahu*), who could possibly describe it?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should know that this Dharma-gate is inconceivable, and its fruit and retribution (*vipāka*) are also inconceivable.
This demonstrates that the essence of that merit and its fruit and retribution cannot be measured; thus, one should know that this Sūtra constitutes a "phrase" (*pada*).

This penetrates both the meaning and the retribution. The "substance of merit" (*puṇya-tattva*) refers to the meaning that is explained; "retribution" (*vipāka*) refers to the result that is experienced.
That which occurs in the present life is called the "fruit of cultivation" (*abhyāsa-phala*); that which is separated by a lifetime is called the "fruit of retribution" (*vipāka-phala*).

15. At the time of realizing the Path, one distances oneself from the agitation of joy. The *Śāstra* states: Among the twelve types [of obstacles], this is for the purpose of distancing oneself from self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*).
The Commentary states: Regarding the "Path of Realization" (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*), one must distinguish between the characteristics of the two teachings.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it refers to those from the first *bhūmi* upward, as they partially realize the Middle Way; for the Treatise says, "at the time of realizing the Path.

In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), it belongs to the stage of the *pariṇāmanā* (dedication), where realization is merely apparent; for the Treatise says, "about to enter realization," implying that one only enters it after bypassing the [preceding] seventeen stages.
Regarding the first stage (*bhūmi*): one may advance or retreat between the two pillars with ease. Now, I say this is not so.

If one were to use the realization of the Way (*praveśa-mārga*) to distinguish between the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], this would undermine the intent of the treatise. The treatise maintains a single underlying meaning; it merely distinguishes between the general and the specific.

If one says that at the time of realizing the Way, this general term refers to the "place of abiding" (*vihāra*), this is simply a formal classification of the text. If one claims that one is about to enter the realization of the Way...
"Etcetera": this is the explanation of the specific text. If that is so, how can one allocate and pair the general and specific texts with the two teachings—the Distinct and the Perfect?
Therefore, there is no basis for such an interpretation. Regarding this, there are two parts; first, the question.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family, who has resolved their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, abide? How should they subdue their minds?"
The *Śāstra* says: "For what reason does he again initiate [this inquiry]? This is the question at the initial stage.
When a Bodhisattva is about to enter the Path of Realization (*darśanamārga*), they perceive for themselves that they have attained a superior state and think:
"I abide thus; I thus subdue my mind; I thus bring sentient beings to parinirvāṇa. To counteract this [conceit], Subhūti asks: "At that time, it should be as follows..."
Abiding. Because the mind has been subdued as described, it is known that emptiness arises at the beginning of the sūtra as the initiating aspect of practice.

Having asked about the matter of subduing and abiding, the Buddha provides the answer for him. The sequence of the stages of practice continues in succession until this point, as one is about to enter the path of realization.

However, fearing that the Bodhisattva might give rise to self-referential attachment—thinking, "I am able to subdue [the mind] and dwell within it," thereby claiming a state of superiority—if such a thought arises, it violates the path of non-abiding and obstructs bodhi.
To serve as an antidote to this, Subhūti asks: "At that very time, when one is entering the realization of the path, since one has already dwelled in prajñā, how could..."
One should take [the mind] oneself; this is for the sake of abandoning such grasping. Therefore, the question arises: "How should one abide? and so forth. As the treatise states:
at the time of realizing the Path, one is far removed from the agitation of joy; it further says, "one is far removed from self-grasping.
Is this not what is meant? Master Zhaoluo said: Subhūti asked again: "What is true abiding and truly subduing the mind? Indeed, Zhaoluo...
The Master’s intention is this: he addresses a bodhisattva who has not yet entered realization, asking about the matter of entering realization, which is termed "true abiding.
Those who compose commentaries do not understand this; they follow their own views and claim that [the practitioner] has already entered realization. Could it really be so? △ Second, the answer.
Furthermore, there are three [parts]. First is the direct answer.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "Good sons and good daughters who have set their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought:
'I should bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa; I shall bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.'"
"Having thus given birth [to this thought], there is not a single sentient being who has truly entered parinirvāṇa.
Below "samyaksaṃbodhi," the word "mind" (citta) is missing; it is likely that the translator omitted the text.
Herein, regarding Subhūti’s initial inquiry and the World-Honored One’s response, it simply says: "One should give rise to such a mind, and then one will be..."
This is the mind that abides in prajñā. One should not give rise to the grasping of a self, nor is there any sentient being to be delivered.

△ Second, the exclusion of what is not [the path]. Why is this? If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, then they are not a bodhisattva.

Śāriputra, since you have not yet entered into realization, ignorance has not been eliminated, and the true principle has not been revealed, there remains the fear that the Bodhisattva might still harbor grasping at a self, a person, and so forth.
In order to examine this thoroughly and thereby exclude such errors, the Treatise states: "If a Bodhisattva [perceives] sentient beings and so on..."

This is to reveal that my retribution-body arises from the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of grasping and delusion; it is precisely consciousness with the latent tendency of ignorance that neither perishes nor ceases.
△ Third, to reveal this:
Why is that? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma whatsoever that sets forth *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding "grasping at the mind," the *Śāstra* states: "If one says, 'I am correctly practicing the Bodhisattva vehicle,' this constitutes grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). To counteract that, the *Sūtra* says:
'Subhūti, in reality, there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva who has resolved upon bodhicitta. (10)

Sixth is for the sake of seeking instruction. The treatise states: among the twelve kinds [of obstacles] based on being free from hindrances, it is for the sake of being free from a lack of instruction that the path is taught and bestowed;
this refers to the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha. This consists of three parts; first, the question.
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, obtain any dharma as anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Having already distanced himself from self-grasping—meaning that, in reality, there is no dharma by which one attains bodhi—the Buddha wished to examine what Śūnyatāputra understood.
He therefore questioned him again using a past event: "What do you think? At that time, when the Tathāgata was practicing his conduct, was there any dharma to be attained or not? 2. The Answer.
"No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
"As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, because the Dharma of Bodhi is ineffable, there was no dharma whatsoever that could be attained from the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
△ Third, the exposition of the fulfillment, which has five parts; first, the formal exposition.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. In truth, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'."
The seal of approval for this teaching was granted; hence it is said, "Thus. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

Subhūti asked the Buddha, "Regarding the mark of non-arising of all dharmas, can one receive the prediction of enlightenment therein? The Buddha replied, "No. He asked again, "Regarding the mark of arising of all dharmas..."
In this regard, is one given the prediction of awakening? The Buddha said, "No. And so on, until:
[Subhūti] asked, "Within the mark of all phenomena being neither arising nor non-arising, is one given the prediction of awakening? The Buddha said, "No. Subhūti said, "World-Honored One..."
"O Bodhisattvas, how do you know that all dharmas receive the prediction of enlightenment? The Buddha said, "Do you see any dharma that receives the prediction of enlightenment?
"No, World-Honored One. I do not see any dharma, nor do I see any recipient of the prediction or any place where it is received.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is. You should know this: this is because the Buddha wishes to demonstrate the non-existence of prajñā."

The characteristics [of his understanding] can be apprehended. Desiring to know what he has realized, the Buddha instead questioned him back. Since Śūnyatā-utpāda’s response accorded with the Buddha’s intent, it was thus confirmed and approved;
this is largely identical in meaning to the present text. △ Second, the negative demonstration (reductio ad absurdum).
Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
then Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
The Treatise says: "If bodhi could be spoken of in the manner that the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara spoke of it, then I would have attained bodhi at that time;
in that case, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara should not have bestowed the prediction upon you, saying, 'In a future age, you shall attain [it]'.
△ Third, returning to the original thesis.
In reality, there is no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me a prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
Why is this? Because "Tathāgata" is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because those phenomena are inexpressible, I did not attain bodhi at that time;
therefore, it should be known that I was granted the prediction [of enlightenment]. Furthermore, why are they inexpressible? Because the Tathāgata arises from true suchness (*bhūtatathatā*).

It comes from within, because the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is all-pervasive; because it is pure like space; and because nothing can be apprehended therein. If anything could be apprehended, it would not be suchness.
Because it would not be suchness, its characteristics would differ, and it could not be called the meaning of the suchness of all phenomena. △ Fourth, guarding against error.
If someone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, Subhūti,
there is in reality no dharma by which the Buddha has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti,
regarding this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata, therein is neither reality nor non-reality.

In this passage, there are three points. "If someone says... and so forth refers to the false grasping at phenomena that do not truly exist; "...free from grasping" refers to the detachment from such grasping.
"That which the Tathāgata has attained... and so forth clarifies this very point. Specifically, "preventing what is non-existent" means preventing that false grasping.
This is answered by the fact that when the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was no dharma by which he attained bodhi; the Buddha himself confirmed this.
"Granted. Regarding the fear that [the meaning] might not be fully understood: this refers to the notion that the Tathāgata did not attain *bodhi* at that time, but attained it later.
Therefore, it says, "If anyone should say... and so forth; such is a false grasping.
To abandon this grasping, it is said that "there is truly no dharma by which a Buddha attains *bodhi*," because such a person speaks untruthfully. Third, this reveals what the Tathāgata has attained.

Regarding Bodhi: within it, there is neither reality nor unreality. The Treatise states it is "without reality," meaning that because it is expressed through verbal discourse, that which has words is not real;

in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it is free from the characteristics of verbal expression. The Treatise states it is "without unreality," meaning that this Bodhi is not non-existent in terms of worldly verbal discourse;
for according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), it possesses the characteristics of verbal expression. This must be understood.
The doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of this sutra discuss only the two truths (*satyadvaya*). The single essence of these two truths is like that of waves and water;

it is because one cannot grasp them as being separate. As the *Śāstra* says: "It reveals that suchness (*tathatā*) is non-dual. "Non-dual" means that the ultimate and the conventional are of one essence.
△ Fifth, the conclusion and demonstration.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. Subhūti, what are called "all dharmas" are not actually all dharmas;
it is for this reason they are called "all dharmas."
The Tathāgata teaches that all dharmas are, in their entirety, true suchness (tathatā). Therefore, it is said that they are all Buddha-dharmas.
Since all dharmas spoken of are of one and the same true suchness, and since true suchness is pure, it is not the dharmas of form and so forth.
Furthermore, because the essence of dharmas is not established, this is for the purpose of establishing the ultimate truth (paramārtha). For this reason, it is called...
Regarding "all dharmas": in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the myriad phenomena are vividly manifest and have never undergone change or transformation.

One must know that, from the perspective of the unchanging essence, all dharmas are entirely *tathatā* (suchness); from the perspective of the functioning that accords with conditions, *tathatā* itself is entirely the myriad dharmas.
There are merely two names, but in reality there are no two essences. How could there be any room for acceptance or rejection? △ Ten.

The seventh is the path of realization (*praveśa-mārga*). Because the preceding twelve types [of paths] all still possess delusive hindrances to be abandoned, this path of realization has already exhausted all obstacles;

it is what is called the "ground of pure mind" (*śuddhāvāsabhūmi*). Within this, there are further two aspects: first, the attainment of wisdom (*jñāna-lābha*); second, the abandonment of pride (*māna-prahāṇa*).
Regarding the first, there are again two parts; the first is the question.
Subhūti, it is like a person whose body has grown large.
"Large" (zhǎngdà) does not mean merely tall; the character *zhǎng* should be pronounced with a rising tone (*shēng*).

This is because, having first resolved upon the mind and practiced through the gradual stages of the path, one has now entered into realization—just as a person grows from childhood to adulthood. Therefore, the Treatise says: "The attainment of wisdom exists."
There are two kinds of wisdom: first, the wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); second, the wisdom of equality.

Once these wisdoms are attained, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata and attains the certainty of succeeding the Buddha-lineage; this constitutes the "encompassing of the spiritual lineage," and so forth.

By analogy with this, the text should be read with the character "cháng" (長) pronounced in the rising tone (*shǎng*). Because of the attainment of wisdom, defilement is transformed, and based upon the pure portion, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are manifested.

As the treatise states: "Having attained this wisdom, one is able to attain the wondrous body (*miao-shen*). In this context, the "wondrous body" refers to the body of attainment (*zhide-shen*) and the body of fulfillment (*chengjiu-shen*).
However, the Sui translation renders it as "wondrous greatness" (*miaoda*), while the present sutra reads "grown great" (*zhangda*);

these are essentially the same. Furthermore, the attainment of wisdom is the retributive wisdom (*baozhi*); attainment is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); and fulfillment is the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Thus, one realizes the three bodies.

Having attained "greatness" (mahat), one realizes the name "Great" (Mahā). Because its essence is pervasive, it is called "Great. Since it cultivates and encompasses the nature [of the lineage], it is said to be the "wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage" (gotra-saṃgrāhaka-jñāna).

Furthermore, there are five kinds of "equality wisdom" (samatājñāna): first, equality regarding coarseness and evil; second, equality regarding the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya); third, equality regarding the application of abandonment;
fourth, equality regarding the application of a mind free from fear and expectation; and fifth, [equality regarding] the application of the non-dual nature of all phenomena.
Fifth, the equality of the realized path of all Bodhisattvas; that is, the identity of their rational nature (li-xing-ti). This is the equality of the three truths. The treatise states:
"Because one attains these equalities, one attains the 'Great Body' (mahākāya), for it encompasses the great bodies of all sentient beings. One must understand this.

Because Bodhisattvas attain this wisdom, they manifest the three bodies (trikāya) and thereby attain a "great body. Sentient beings also inherently possess the three bodies, which is likewise called a "great body.
Since the substance of the three bodies is one, cultivation is fully realized through nature, and cultivation subsumes nature;
therefore, it is said that they "subsume the great body of sentient beings. △ Second, the answer.
Subhūti said, “World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being large, it is precisely because it is not a large body that it is called a ‘large body.
The Tathāgata reveals the great body attained through entering and realizing the Way, which encompasses the principle of all sentient beings and constitutes a great body.”

Question: Śūnyatā-utpanna (Empty-born) answers by distinguishing between the nature (*prakṛti*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This constitutes the exclusion of what is not the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*).

Regarding the exclusion of the nature, the *Śāstra* states: "Within that body, one establishes that which is neither self nor other. Now, "that" refers to the body of sentient beings. "Not self" means it is not the *vipāka-kāya* (retribution body);
"not other" means it is not the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body). Although the three bodies are complete within the body of a sentient being, [the text proceeds to distinguish them].
Having not yet generated the mind [of awakening] or engaged in application, one possesses only the *dharmakāya* that is concordant with the correct nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Since it lacks the "great body" subsumed under the *vipākakāya* and *nairmāṇikakāya*, it is therefore not a "great body. As for what is called the "great body," this reveals cultivation. The treatise states:
"Within this great body, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is established. Furthermore, this "great body" refers to the Bodhisattvas who have entered into realization.
Regarding the great body of those sentient beings, it is said: "Within this great body, the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is established;
thus, the three bodies (trikāya) are fully possessed. This is called the 'great body. The Treatise states: "Such as these constitute the attainment of wisdom.
△ Second, the abandonment of pride, which has two parts. First, the absence of pride.
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva. If one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then that person is not called a bodhisattva.

The preceding passage refers to the attainment of wisdom; this section refers to the elimination of pride (*māna*). Since one has already eliminated pride, it manifests the state of non-recollection (*amanasikāra*).

The Treatise states: "If one forms the thought, 'I liberate sentient beings,' or 'I am a Bodhisattva,' one should know that such a person is one possessed of pride and is not a Bodhisattva in the true sense. 2. Returning to the Main Thesis.

Why is this? Subhūti, there is truly no dharma that can be called a "bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha has said that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span.

Because they do not grasp for themselves—meaning that these bodhisattvas likewise have no sentient beings to deliver, as they have eliminated both subject and object—it is said that "in reality, there is no dharma called 'bodhisattva'.
Citing the Buddha’s words as proof, the Buddha taught that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma;
thus, there are no marks of a self, a dharma, a person, or others. Therefore, the Treatise says: "If a bodhisattva..."
If sentient beings harbor such thoughts, they shall not attain the wondrous, great body. △ Eighteenth:

Regarding the upward seeking of the Buddha-ground, one should know that there are further six kinds of perfection which encompass the perfection of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). These are: first, the perfection of the purity of the land;

second, the perfection of the purity of supreme vision and wisdom; third, the perfection of mastery over merit; fourth, the perfection of the body; fifth, the perfection of speech; [and sixth, the perfection of mind].
Sixth, the perfection of mind. The commentary states: "As for 'transformation of the basis' (āśraya-parāvṛtti), it means transforming the defiled and relying upon the pure.
Because during the nine stages all phenomena depend upon the ālayavijñāna, their respective lands, as well as the three karmas, were entirely defiled and obstructed.
Now, having reached the state of fruition, since the ālaya has been destroyed, one transforms all phenomena so that they rely upon [the pure basis]."
Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, from the buddha-field down to the three karmas, all are entirely pure. Regarding the term "complete" (*paripūrṇa*):
by means of this transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which integrates the preceding realization of the path, one now seeks upward toward the ultimate completion of the Buddha-ground.

Based on this, there are six [types of completeness]. However, these six kinds of completeness do not transcend the two types of retribution: the environment and the body. The buddha-field belongs to the environment; the latter five belong to the body.
This pertains to the perfection of the purity of the buddha-field. Furthermore, there are two parts.
First, the exclusion of what is not [the true path]. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn a buddha-field," he is not called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? When the Tathāgata speaks of adorning buddha-fields, it is not actually adornment; it is designated as "adornment. The Commentary states:
"This is because [the mind] functions within the sphere of common perception and correct practice; therefore, in order to sever that [perception], the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is established.
One must understand that adorning the buddha-field is itself correct practice. If one were to say, "I am able to adorn..."
To "adorn the Buddha-lands" involves the coexistence of subject and object, giving rise to the view of conceptual discrimination; therefore, it is called a "shared view.
Such a person is not named a Bodhisattva, because they deviate from right practice. In order to sever that conceptual grasping, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is established.
Within the ultimate truth, although one may adorn the Buddha-lands, one does not grasp at that adornment.
[The Buddha said: "What do you think? Why is this? In the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, there is adornment without being adorned.
2. Revealing the True [Bodhisattva]: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and dharmas, the Tathāgata calls him by the name of a 'true bodhisattva'."

The Treatise says: "One who penetrates selflessness" refers to two kinds of selflessness, namely, the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

By contrast, it is revealed that if there is grasping at the two kinds of self—namely, the thought "I have accomplished [this]" being grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-grāha*), and the thought "adorned is the land" being grasping at a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātma-grāha*)—then this is not a bodhisattva. 2. The Perfection of the Purity of Vision and Wisdom. The Treatise says:

It is said: One establishes "vision" (*darśana*) for the sake of realizing the true reality within; one establishes "knowledge" (*jñāna*) for the sake of teaching those sentient beings to pacify their minds.
This is the single essence of the five eyes seeing the one mind and the three knowledges.

To realize the five eyes and bodhi through knowing the true reality within is one's own practice (*sva-caryā*). To teach those sentient beings to abide in the mind of the three knowledges is [the practice for others].
This concerns the transformation of others. The text is divided into two parts.
First, regarding the purity of vision: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "So it is, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye. "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "So it is, World-Honored One. So forth.
"Subhūti, does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom eye?
Subhūti, he does, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma eye? Subhūti, he does, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha eye?"
"No. It is so, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.

However, throughout this sutra from beginning to end, there is nothing that does not eliminate conceptual signs (*nimitta*). Why is it that only in this passage does Subhūti fully answer that the Tathāgata possesses the five eyes?
One must understand that the elimination of signs is certainly not absent; it is explained concurrently in the subsequent text. But here..."
What is the intent behind the detailed response? It is because the *prajñāpāramitā* can give rise to the five eyes;
it is specifically to manifest this that the response is given in detail. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Of the six *pāramitās*, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the foundation."
For this reason, it is said that the *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the five eyes. As the bodhisattva gradually studies these five eyes, he will before long become a Buddha.
From this, one knows that [the present stage] reaches the ground of Buddhahood; this is to manifest that the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the five eyes.
The treatise states: "The Tathāgata does not possess only the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*); [this is taught] in order to show that his knowledge and vision are pure and supreme."
Therefore, it is shown that there are five kinds of eyes. If it were otherwise, one would merely seek the pure vision of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

However, if one eliminates all marks and clarifies emptiness, this should be what is seen by the wisdom-eye; yet for a Tathāgata, it is not limited to the wisdom-eye alone, but possesses all five eyes.
As the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-samantamukha-parivarta* states: "By being fully endowed with the five eyes, one accomplishes Bodhi. For this reason, the Tathāgata is possessed of [all five].

Question: Śūnyatā-utpanna (Empty-Born) answered in full detail. Had he not answered in full detail, the Bodhisattva practicing *prajñāpāramitā* would not have achieved the five eyes for the sake of awakening (*bodhi*).
Therefore it is said: "If it were otherwise, one would merely seek the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) to see the pure.

The *Śāstra* states: "Within this, briefly stated, there are four kinds of eyes: namely, those comprised by form (*rūpa*), those comprised by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and [those comprised by] the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)."
[It is] subsumed. It is subsumed by all aspects of all that is to be known. Furthermore, the subsumption of form (*rūpa*) is twofold.

First, there is that which is the fruit of cultivation within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because this is the coarse object-field of the five eyes, it constitutes the primary subsumption of form.

Thus, one knows that the meaning of the five eyes encompasses the ten dharma-realms. "Fruit" refers to the fruit of cultivation; cultivation pertains to the phenomenal (*vastu*), and this [fruit] constitutes the coarse object-field.

Because it belongs to the realm (*dhātu*), it is subsumed under form (*rūpa*). Second, because of the power of the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*), worldly knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) functions without inversion;

this is explained by way of the identity of the substance of these two knowledges. [The former] is subsumed under the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the latter is subsumed under the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
thus, the meaning is distinguished. The five eyes possessed by the Tathāgata are not actually divided; they are simply one.
The eye possesses five functions and is able to illuminate five objects. Although the four eyes share a common cause and see the same things, the Buddha’s vision transcends what they see;
therefore, it is subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding the fourth point, "subsumption under all aspects of all that should be known":
this refers to the Dharma-eye. As the treatise states: "Among these, he teaches the Dharma to people; if that Dharma is for that person..."
This is explained as the gift of Dharma. This stage is called the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).
